entries.title: 2 fatally shot in Hyde Park
entries.summary: <p>Two people were fatally shot Thursday afternoon in Hyde Park, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A 24-year-old man and 27-year-old woman were found inside a vehicle in the 5900 block of East Ellis Avenue at 5:35 p.m. with single gunshot wounds to each of their heads, police said. They were both taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where they later died.</p><p>A dark sedan crashed on the east curb of Ellis Avenue with damage to its front, its airbags deployed and both front doors open. About a dozen officers processed the scene and put up red tape around 7 p.m.</p><p>No one was in custody.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man killed, 13-year-old boy shot in West Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was killed and a boy hospitalized by a shooting in West Garfield Park Thursday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Two men fired shots at 6:50 p.m. in the 3800 block of West Adams Street, hitting a 49-year-old man on the sidewalk and a 13-year-old boy in a car, police said. The man was taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital where he later died.</p><p>The boy was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was listed in good condition, police said.</p><p>No one is in custody.<br></p>

entries.title: Pullman to celebrate century anniversary of Metra Electric line
entries.summary: <p>Historic railcars and interactive exhibits will be showcased this week in Pullman on the city's South Side to help celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Metra Electric line.</p><p>Officials made the announcement Thursday at a news conference at the Millennium Station Downtown.</p><p>The Railroad Days celebration, 10 a.m.- 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday at Pullman Historical National Park, will feature a restored 1926 Pullman electric railcar and a vintage 1970s-era railcar. Visitors also can explore model train displays; a science, technology, engineering, art and math fair with hands-on science and engineering activities; food trucks; live music and presentations. Tickets are $20 before Saturday and $25 on Saturday and Sunday.</p><p>Friends of Pullman Executive Director Peggy Parfenoff said the transition from steam-powered locomotives to electric rail service helped transform the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2d0000" entries.title: Man sitting in vehicle fatally shot in Uptown
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot early Friday while sitting in a vehicle in Uptown.</p><p>The 21-year-old man was in the vehicle in the 5100 block of North Winthrop Avenue around 12:25 a.m. when someone approached and opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was shot in the neck and taken to the Illinois Masonic Medical Center, where he died, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: 2 shot, 1 fatally, in Hyde Park
entries.summary: <p>Two people were shot, one fatally, Thursday night in Hyde Park.</p><p>Around 11:10 p.m., a 25-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were in a parked vehicle in the 5400 block of South Shore Drive when a vehicle drove by and someone inside that vehicle opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man was shot in the abdomen and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died, police said. </p><p>The woman was shot in the shoulder and was taken to the same hospital in fair condition. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Memorial to Burge torture victims is about acknowledging pain, healing
entries.summary: <p>Public memorials reflect whom a city chooses to remember. Memorializing ugly historical truths is a chance for public healing. Chicago is reckoning with both.</p><p>Earlier this month, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandon-johnson/2026/07/08/johnson-breaks-ground-on-long-awaited-memorial-to-burge-torture-victims" >city broke ground</a> on a decade-old promise — the <a class="Link" href="https://ctjmfoundation.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Torture Justice Memorial</a>, a permanent structure in the Washington Park neighborhood recognizing survivors of police torture under former Chicago Police Cmdr. Jon Burge. For 20 years, beginning in 1973,<a class="Link" href="https://www.themarshallproject.org/2018/10/30/payback" target="_blank" > Burge and other police officers at the Area 2 station beat, suffocated and electrically shocked </a>more than 100 Black and Brown folks for dirty confessions. Once completed, the concrete circular structure will include a timeline and names of survivors.</p><p>Anthony Holmes is a survivor and reparations recipient who advocated for the memorial. </p><p>“This is everything we've been trying to tell people. This is our truth,” Holmes said. When the monument is completed next year, neighbors “can feel it and enjoy it, even though it's got a lot of sadness in it.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-990000" name="module-990000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>In 2015, the City Council passed a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2015/5/6/18588336/city-council-approves-5-5-million-in-reparations-for-burge-torture-victims" >reparations ordinance</a> that awarded Burge survivors an apology from the city, a pool of money, mental health therapy and free tuition to city colleges for them and family members. Chicago Public Schools eighth graders and 10th graders learn about the Burge saga.</p><p>Now the final piece of the package is the nation’s first permanent remembrance to survivors of police torture. The timing was delayed but now opportune.</p><p>As the country celebrates 250 years of the Declaration of Independence, democracy is fragile. Commemorative T-shirts, fireworks and waxing about American exceptionalism are on full patriotic display. All men (not to mention women) were not considered equal to have life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in 1776. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/ending-radical-indoctrination-in-k-12-schooling/" target="_blank" >The Trump administration labels history</a> as anti-American ideology in K-12 classrooms. White supremacists and their allies push for book bans, stripping college curriculum and <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/22/house-gop-national-history-museum-director-01008134" target="_blank" >attacking scholars</a> — anything critical of the United States. Ignoring the truth about this country is unpatriotic. The memorial to Burge torture victims isn’t.</p><p>“We are proud that here in Chicago. We are actually being honest about that past, and that in and of itself is something to celebrate. And we're grateful that so many people in Chicago are on board with that and understand how important that is,” said Jen Ash, executive director at the Chicago Torture Justice Memorial Foundation.</p><p>The fight for justice incorporated art in its early days of radical imagination. An exhibition of memorial proposals<a class="Link" href="https://chicagocrusader.com/chicago-torture-justice-memorial-to-be-built-in-washington-park/" target="_blank" > in 2019</a> showcased six submissions from commissioned artists. The winner of "Still Here: Torture, Resiliency, and the Art of Memorializing” exhibition was the team consisting of artist Patricia Nguyen and architectural designer John Lee. Chicago architect John Gay will lead construction of the $4.7 million memorial based on the duo's design. </p><p>In 2020, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2021/03/11/the-chicago-monuments-project-grapples-with-the-hard-history-of-some-city-statues" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago</u></a> and other cities around the country evaluated how to manage the racist symbolism of public statues. Public sentiment no longer desired for confederate tributes, odes to segregationists and honoring colonizers. The Mellon Foundation — which assisted financially for the Chicago Torture Justice Memorial — is funding other <a class="Link" href="https://www.mellon.org/article/engaging-physical-history-and-mending-community-wounds" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago projects</u></a> such as honoring gospel legend Mahalia Jackson and marking the 1919 race riots. Commissioning new landmarks is an opportunity to use physical public history for engagement, because tearing down a Christopher Columbus statue isn’t enough. But erecting a memorial to Chicagoans who endured unfathomable abuse is a start. And is aligned with democracy.</p><p><i>Natalie Y. Moore is a senior lecturer at Northwestern University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband's career struggles impact couple's marriage
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married for 11 years and have two children. When we met, he worked two union jobs, paid his bills, saved his money and took care of his mother and grandmother when they needed his financial support. About six years ago, he decided he didn't want to work with the union anymore, and I supported him in exploring alternative career paths. He has tried currency trading, personal training and used car sales. Nothing seems to stick.</p><p>I work five days a week and have a part-time job on the weekends to bring in extra income. We are unable to make ends meet, and my extended family often has to bail us out because we can't pay our bills. I told my husband I need him to start making a decent income again. He said he would, but I see little effort from him in terms of gaining solid employment.</p><p>Our relationship is not going well. I have lost faith in him. I want to stay together, but I need him to provide for his family. I don't know how much more of this I can tolerate. Please help. — <i>OVERWORKED AND UNDERWHELMED</i></p><p><b>DEAR O & U:</b> Your husband has gotten comfortable with letting you do the heavy lifting in the family. If you don't give him specific goals and deadlines, he's not likely to clean up his act.</p><p>State the exact monthly income you need him to provide, even if he ends up working several part-time jobs to do so. Then give him a certain number of job applications he must complete each day. If he doesn't reach these goals by a certain date, the next step will be separation. This may seem harsh, but remember that you and your kids are suffering because he isn't pulling his weight.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married to a wonderful man for 36 years. During the last 12 years, he has had heart surgery and some depression. He refuses to get out of his easy chair and do anything. He won't bathe or shower and insists that washing off in the sink is good enough. He smells, and I'm embarrassed to go places with him because of it.</p><p>I have tried to encourage him and let him know how I love a clean-scented man. He just doesn't care. I won't even kiss him. He refuses to help around the house and expects me to do everything. I still work, and we are raising a granddaughter. I'm no longer in love with him but I do love him. I have wanted a divorce for a while now, but, financially, I can't afford to live on my own. Thank you for any advice. — <i>ALL WASHED UP</i></p><p><b>DEAR ALL WASHED UP:</b> You need to discuss this with a doctor who can advise you about the options for treating depression and apathy after heart surgery, as well as an attorney who can help you determine if enough assets have been acquired during your 36-year marriage to allow you to live independently. Once you have that information, you may be able to give your husband an ultimatum and force him out of the easy chair and into a healthier lifestyle, which could add years to his life.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>What teens need to know about sex, drugs, AIDS and getting along with peers and parents is in "What Every Teen Should Know." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Teen Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Remembering victims of 1919 Chicago race riot: 38 names set in stone
entries.summary: <p>As Chicago celebrates the opening of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/18/obama-presidential-center-opening-jackson-park" >Obama Presidential Center</a>, our city is embracing a renewed sense of possibility. At nearly the same moment, another remarkable civic milestone quietly reached completion.</p><p>Across Chicago, all 38 people killed during the Chicago race riot of 1919 are now permanently commemorated through public art installed at or near the places they lost their lives.</p><p>These two milestones are different in purpose, but deeply connected in meaning. One is encouraging us to imagine our future, while the <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/chicagoraceriot.org/__;!!MyIu0v6UfBA57LoN!4e0dPTKnR2VHhQQ0_4xOl7h8KCV0QA0pw87hwQ78VTdTZYoiQmjB5jLDeciFydLbSdEe5isSa3yzz3S0Src-YXVgNWfMg75B$" target="_blank" >Chicago Race Riot of 1919 Commemoration Project</a> asks us to confront our past.</p><p>Together, they remind us that remembering history is not the same as reckoning with it.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-df0000" name="module-df0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>More than a century has passed since the race riot in 1919, yet its legacy continues to shape the city we know today. </p><p>The story begins with five Black children seeking relief from the summer heat in Lake Michigan. What could be more Chicago than that?</p><p>When the children unknowingly crossed an invisible racial boundary in the water, a white man began throwing rocks. One struck 17-year-old Eugene Williams, who drowned. A white police officer refused to arrest the man responsible. </p><p>Anger spread. Rumors spread faster. Within hours, violence engulfed Chicago. By week's end, 38 people had been killed, more than 500 injured, and over 1,000, primarily Black folks, had been left homeless.</p><p>When we ask why Chicago remains one of America's most segregated cities, the answer cannot begin with redlining. It began in 1919 with residential segregation accelerating through restrictive covenants, and it laid the foundation for the redlining, predatory housing contracts, disinvestment and unequal development that still defines much of Chicago.</p><p>Our city’s collective historical amnesia was precisely why, on the centennial of the murder of Eugene Williams, several hundred people convened in Bronzeville to remember. That community event inspired the creation of the <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/chicagoraceriot.org/__;!!MyIu0v6UfBA57LoN!4e0dPTKnR2VHhQQ0_4xOl7h8KCV0QA0pw87hwQ78VTdTZYoiQmjB5jLDeciFydLbSdEe5isSa3yzz3S0Src-YXVgNWfMg75B$" target="_blank" >Chicago Race Riot of 1919 Commemoration Project</a>.</p><p>Our vision was simple: Every person who lost their life should be remembered where they lost it. It is now a reality. The installation of the memorials means that for the first time in Chicago's history, every person killed during the riot has a permanent place in our public landscape.</p><p>The completion of all 38 memorial markers represents the culmination of more than six years of collaboration among artists, historians, educators, community partners and residents committed to preserving this history</p><p>The memorials are scattered across nearly 30 square miles of Chicago, from the lakefront to Bronzeville, Bridgeport, Englewood, Washington Park, Back of the Yards, Little Italy and the Loop.</p><p>Public art possesses a unique power. Public art works 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 52 weeks a year, year-in and year-out and “finds” people not looking to be educated, inspired or provoked. That’s the genius.</p><p>The memorials were created through an extraordinary partnership with the city’s Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events, Chicago Monuments Project, Mellon Foundation, Organic Oneness and Firebird Community Arts’ nationally recognized Project FIRE, where young people affected by gun violence researched each victim and handcrafted every marker from glass. </p><p>Each marker is intentionally shaped like a brick, a painful reminder of one of the weapons commonly used during the violence of 1919.</p><p>Like so many other Chicagoans, none of the youth artists previously knew this history. Today they’ve helped to cement this history, literally, into our city’s sidewalks for generations to discover.</p><p>Our signature annual event tells the history and legacy of 1919 and celebrates the resilience and beauty of Chicago’s Black community. This year's event will happen on Saturday, when Chicagoans will gather at the lakefront, where there are two memorials, including one for Eugene Williams, to begin our annual commemoration and community bike ride. </p><p>We invite you to join us and visit one marker or all 38, read the names, learn their stories, walk these neighborhoods, and bring your children and neighbors. Go to <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoraceriot.org/" target="_blank" >chicagoraceriot.org</a> for more information.</p><p>Because every one of those 38 lives mattered, join us so we can grow awareness, build community and keep the historical memory alive.</p><p>For too long, silence defined this chapter of Chicago's history, but as South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission <a class="Link" href="https://sahistory.org.za/archive/truth-hurts-silence-kills" target="_blank" >noted</a>, “The truth hurts but silence kills.”</p><p>Today, through 38 memorial markers across our city, truth has finally found a permanent home.</p><p><i>Peter Cole, Franklin Cosey-Gay, Dunni Cosey-Gay and Myles X. Francis together lead the Chicago Race Riot of 1919 Commemoration Project, a community-led initiative dedicated to researching, commemorating and educating the public about the Chicago Race Riot of 1919 through public art, education and civic engagement. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9e0000" name="module-9e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Black-crowned night heron love spreading their wings in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Fox32 Chicago's <a class="Link" href="https://www.fox32chicago.com/news/rare-state-endangered-bird-spotted-downtown-chicago-goes-viral" target="_blank" >recent segment</a> about a young black-crowned night heron perched on a River North window ledge was a fun story. But it also revealed something surprising: Most viewers had no idea that a state-endangered bird has chosen to make Chicago home.</p><p>For two decades, they have returned each spring to nest in Lincoln Park, raising their young in the heart of one of America's largest cities. Their numbers tell an important story. In 1992, an estimated peak of more than 1,600 adult black-crowned night herons were recorded in the Calumet region. This year, the colony reached a peak count of approximately 455 adults, a stark contrast to the historic Calumet numbers and a reminder of the challenges these birds face.</p><p>Despite the challenges they face, the herons continue to choose Chicago. They continue to raise their chicks here, forage along our rivers, lagoons and lakefront, and remind us that wildlife can still thrive in an urban landscape when we make room for it.</p><p>For the past three years, volunteers with the Chicago Black-crowned Night Heron Project have met thousands of people who were amazed to learn these remarkable birds live among us. Their reaction is almost always the same: "I had no idea."</p><p>Perhaps that's the real story. These herons haven't given up on Chicago. They're still here, waiting for us to notice them and to recognize that their future in Illinois depends, in part, on the choices we make today.</p><p><i>Amy Lardner, founder, Chicago Black-crowned Night Heron Project</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-750000" name="module-750000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Good and bad sportsmanship </h3><p>Last weekend’s golf and soccer championships proved again that sports are a reflection of life. </p><p>The Good: Ryan Fox, who won the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/ryan-fox-notah-begay-mazzoli-fedex-cup-1bf3f6164391af94098de60a7d007ff7" target="_blank" >British Open</a>, coped with two horribly bad breaks on the finishing holes with equanimity. Under great pressure, he had the courage and ability to win with a birdie on the brutally difficult final hole.</p><p>The Bad: Bryson DeChambeau whined like a petulant <a class="Link" href="https://www.si.com/golf/british-open/bryson-dechambeau-needs-to-stop-acting-like-such-a-child" target="_blank" >child</a> about British Open rules, thereby considerably delaying the entire field, and apparently threatened to withdraw from the event and/or to enlist the <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jul/20/bryson-dechambeau-donald-trump-open-championshiup-penalty-golf-royal-birkdale" target="_blank" >aid of Donald Trump</a>, who has a history of meddling in sporting events and has demonstrated on and off the golf course his belief that if one is not cheating, one is not competing.</p><p>The Ugly: A tie between Trump, who tried to elbow his way into Spanish team’s victory celebration in the World Cup, and the Argentina team's disregard for <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/world-cup-final-brawl-scuffle-paredes-96a47e04a3485874b808a0ebcd90c76a" target="_blank" >sportsmanship and civility</a> after the match.</p><p>These are lessons to be learned about how and how not to behave.</p><p><i>William P. Gottschalk, Lake Forest</i> </p><h3>Perseverance on parade</h3><p>I work in a snack shop in Chicago that is owned by a visually challenged man. His disability has never stopped him from pursuing his dreams. There are thousands like him. It will be their moment to shine at Saturday's <a class="Link" href="https://www.disabilityprideparade.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Disability Pride Parade</a>. They deserve it.</p><p><i>Terrence Camodeca, Orland Park</i></p><h3>Close 4 a.m. bars </h3><p>After the closure of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/22/lincoln-park-the-dime-knudsen-o-neill-burke" >the Dime in Lincoln Park</a>, it’s time for the city to outlaw 4 a.m. liquor licenses. Those bars have long been a source of crime, and there’s no justification for allowing them to serve alcohol that late. The only justification is money the bar owners "donate" to City Council members.</p><p><i>Tom Vega-Byrnes, Beverly</i></p>

entries.title: What can parents do in the age of AI? A new book has ideas
entries.summary: <p>Artificial intelligence has the potential to alter the lifelong hardwiring of future generations if given to kids younger than 6, leaving them ill-equipped to navigate human relationships, sustain the attention required for learning and making it more difficult to develop empathy.</p><p>That assessment — found in Dr. Dana Suskind’s new book, “Human Raised: Nurturing Connection, Curiosity, & Lifelong Learning in the Age of AI” — makes handwringing over screentime and social media look almost quaint in comparison.</p><p>In her third book, Dr. Suskind outlines how these emerging technologies are disruptive to a developing brain and offers guidelines for parents on how to assess whether (or which ones) to allow their children to use.</p><p>AI shows up for this younger age group in cribs enhanced with technology to offer parents troves of sleep data; smart tutors to work on language development skills in preschools or digital read alouds for storytime; and plushie companions that can greet a child by name, tell bedtime stories, and "remember" facts about their "friend."</p><p>Suskind, professor of surgery and pediatrics at the University of Chicago, and co-director at the TMW Center for Early Learning and Public Health, has dedicated her career to child development and parenting.</p><p>When I talked to Suskind recently, I admitted right off the bat that I feel totally at sea about how to navigate AI as a parent. My gut instinct is to say, I don’t understand it, I don’t like it, and to run screaming from the room. We already parented through a pandemic, now we have to figure this out, too?</p><p>Because she has spent her entire career navigating questions from parents like me – as she told me later, “parents are really my heart” – she was sympathetic. Her book even luckily provides an easy assessment framework that even the least tech savvy among us can handle.</p><p>What followed was a long conversation about how to navigate parenting amid these new technologies, how the onus is on parents in the absence of regulations, and how “good enough” parenting – the kind where parents are present and engaged as their imperfect selves – is actually ideal for human development. This conversation was adapted for length and clarity.</p><hr><p><b>Rebecca Little: As you write, the relationship between child development and AI “has the potential to transform childhood, family structures, and ultimately nothing less than our future as a species.” Can you talk about what makes artificial intelligence so uniquely transformative to early childhood?</b></p><p><b>Dr. Dana Suskind</b>: This is truly the first technology that can mimic human interaction. We’re a very social species. The drive to connect is as primitive as the drive to eat. Connection and relationships are how we stayed alive and developed as a species. Now we have these technologies that can replicate it, and it’s going to seem like a relationship, especially to a young brain. And this relationship will be so much easier than messy, difficult human relationships which could make their brains unaccustomed or unable to navigate them, or prefer the seamless interaction with technology.</p><p><b>Babies are born with neurons that have to be connected through early experiences, and if it doesn’t happen, those neurons are pruned away. Kids are developing skills from age 0 to six that hardwire them forever. Let’s talk more about the importance of this early neuroplasticity.</b></p><p>It’s mostly understanding how humans develop relationships. I come from the world of child development, so I study the importance of language and interaction. I have seen the impact of language – that particular input, the nurturing interaction from parents – is a way to build the hard skills of language and literacy. But the biggest aha moment was understanding that it was also building social and emotional and relationship skills – the ability to really relate to other humans.</p><p>Babies are born way too early. Human babies are born with brains only one-third the size of the adult-size brain, and that’s different from any other species. Horses and dogs have almost adult- sized brains, which is why they can be so independent early on. The fact that we were born so early is both a huge opportunity and a huge risk.</p><p>Nurturing interaction feeds the brain, and is also the instruction guide for how to wire up the brain for the world that child is going to be living in. There's more brain activity at that period of time than any other time – a million neural connections are formed every second from every snuggle, every word spoken in parentese, etcetera. But the brain starts pruning away the connections that aren’t used in order to be more efficient.</p><p>Part and parcel to this is the attachment phenomenon. Babies attach to adult caregivers for protection. It teaches babies what relationships look like. The risk of artificial attachment with these devices could change what a child expects from relationships. With “good enough” parenting, you've got someone who loves you, sometimes they mess up, sometimes they're not happy with you, but it's still going to be OK, and you learn to have a relationship with another human being who's got all their imperfections. But with artificial attachment, in theory, it's like having someone who's always there, who's always responsive, but who says you're always right, and it’s just so easy. And that will teach you something distinctly different about what relationships should look like.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dr. Suskind shared that essential skills are shaped by human interaction: deep connection, critical thinking, creativity, resilience, curiosity and the ability to read a room. Here, Mallory Seliga and her daughter Maisie Seliga watch a performer play with a dropper during “RAIN: For Babies and Their Carers” at Filament Theatre.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>What seems especially challenging is that parents have to learn to parent their kids in the time of AI and also prepare the kid for a world that will be altered by it. Those are two different challenges that are happening in real time. What are the ways in which parents can do both of those things? </b></p><p>What is so clear is that those two things, parenting in the age of AI and parenting for the age of AI, bring you to the same conclusion: human connection and messy relationships are the right answer. It’s actually the most beautiful thing that in the most technologic advanced moment in human history, the skills you’re really going to need are distinctly human skills: deep connection, critical thinking, creativity, resilience, curiosity and the ability to read a room. Those are built by human interaction.</p><p>Now, technology can do all of those hard skills that we’ve been optimizing our kids for, but having empathy can’t be optimized. It can only be built by human presence, repetition, and messy human interactions. Technology has already been slowly eroding our ability to connect with each other, but this is a wake up call. We have to double down on connecting and understanding each other. It’’s hard, but that friction is what makes us stay human.</p><p><b>Over the last maybe 30 years – whenever helicopter parenting or snowplow parenting became common terms – there was already criticism about kids raised with minimal friction, like kids arriving at college having never done a chore. We already know kids need some challenges and independence to learn how to be a person, but AI has the potential to make that journey to age 18 a skating rink.</b></p><p>Parenting is the hardest job. Snowplow or tiger parenting was a rational response to that moment in time. There was huge inequality in the U.S. and huge returns on education, so why not optimize so your kid can get into the best preschool, get the highest test score, or get into the best college? But I wonder if now parenting will be about presence, about “good enough” parenting, and maybe it will break the spell of “intensive” parenting.</p><p>Being present, being imperfect, is the best thing – just being yourself, loving your kid, and messing up. My children are young adults now, and I can tell you, I was just the perfect imperfect parent. Back then, I felt so much guilt. I’m a working mom, there was always so much going on at once. Now that I've written this book, I'm like, hmm, I helped you with my imperfect parenting. You're welcome. [laughs]</p><p><b>I thought the same. I have unintentionally been practicing “good enough” parenting for the last 16 years. So I did it, kids! You’re all set. I often sound like an old lady talking about, “back in my day, we rode our bikes and watched VHS tapes, and when the movie was over, we went back outside!” But it’s not just yearning for a childhood that we as parents understand – it’s feeling daunted by having to navigate one unprecedented thing after another, mostly without an instruction manual. You have created framework called HOPE, which gives parents a simple assessment for whether a child should be allowed to interact with a certain technology. How do we use it?</b></p><p>It’s based on developmental science. H is that human connection is irreplaceable. It’s not just a nice to have, it’s a biological necessity and the number one thing to protect. So you have to ask, is this technology crowding that out or supporting it? O is for owning your imperfections, the power of friction and good enough parenting for building your child’s brain. P is for protecting the early years when you’re building the actual hardware of the brain; parents need to be super careful about this technology. Lastly E is for enhance, not replace. I am not anti-technology at all. I'm a cochlear implant surgeon. I've seen the power of technology. But it should enhance our experiences. So if it lightens the parental load or offers up data, fine, but when AI replaces human interaction, it’s a risk. The simple HOPE framework is evergreen, and that's something that you can go back to even as technology advances.</p><p><b>That’s what I found so reassuring about your book. This all seems very overwhelming, but a four-letter framework is doable without having to figure out each new technology, and being a “good enough” parent is extremely doable. But there’s an even more succinct method: As you point out, a lot of the people who built these systems do not let their children use them. It seems an easy shorthand for a parent gatekeeper – does the person who invented it, use it?</b></p><p>Exactly. If you’re not sure what to do, just look at the tech titans and model what they’re using because if they’re not, that’s an important data point.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dr. Suskind’s HOPE framework gives parents a simple assessment for whether a child should be allowed to interact with a certain technology.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Dr. Dana Suskind</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>It’s not just screen time that we have to track anymore; it’s that so much of what kids are consuming is AI slop on YouTube, some of which is labeled educational. My kids sometimes use Siri to get a quick answer. But a lot of these systems use faulty sources – like Google AI assist – are citing Reddit, so now some dude who tossed off an opinion from his couch is a leading authority?</b></p><p>The slop is at an unprecedented scale. There's always been misinformation, but it's just so scalable now. I talk about Fred Rogers [Mr. Rogers from PBS] a little bit in the book, and he said he went into television because he hated it so much. What he meant was that it wasn’t necessarily the medium, it was the quality of the content being served up. We already know this fast content, these dopamine hits, are not good for our kids, but it’s also full of misinformation. These videos teach kids the wrong ABCs and how to count incorrectly. Shouldn't somebody be responsible if my kid learns the ABCs wrong? If you've mistaught a whole generation of humans, who is accountable?</p><p><b>The potential to rewire a child’s brain seems like a four-alarm regulatory fire to me, but so far, there are very few regulations dealing with much of big tech at all. Why is it falling on parents to sort it out? </b></p><p>We're at the beginning of this tech revolution. There are relatively few guardrails, and I'm hoping over time that we get them. Can you imagine if you went to the grocery store and said, I wonder if this candy has arsenic in it. I guess I'll bring it home and try to figure it out myself. We're putting so much on the humans. Beyond basic privacy rules, we need tiers of regulation based on the type of AI content. A technology that helps a teacher develop a lesson plan is very different from a technology that a kid is working with directly. I hope with the greater awareness now of the dangers of social media and screentime that we won’t sleepwalk into this next period. Young childhood will not wait.</p><p><b>A book ends, a show ends, but the algorithm on YouTube is designed to keep kids watching and suggest clip after clip. I’m sure most parents have had the experience of their child turning into Gollum when taking a screen away. Current AI and tech is focused on the attention economy, but what’s coming next is the “intimacy economy” built on trust and the human need to be loved, which is so much harder to disengage from.</b></p><p>Children are even more likely to anthropomorphize a robot or technology. We have a drive to connect with a caregiver for protection which is probably why the earlier you get these technologies, the more likely you are to connect with them in that way, to ascribe human qualities to it. But these devices can’t care, they’re just set up to mimic caring.</p><p>Technology, when designed the right way, can lead to human flourishing and to address so many of things I’ve been working on in my career to support parents. AI is analogous to artificial food. On the one side is whole wheat bread and canned foods that still remain nourishing. The food revolution led to a decrease in malnutrition, to growing cities so people could get off the farm and become educated, and a lot of good came of it. What happened over time is [the development of] ultraprocessed, cheap alternatives that stimulated our dopamine receptors and are hyper palatable. It’s frictionless in the same way AI can be.</p><p>With AI, I look at the things that are really helpful or that lift administrative burdens off parents. Parents want to parent. We didn’t have children because we didn’t want to be around them. It’s the realities of society that made it so. Tech that lifts burdens on the logistic side could clear the way so parents can be more present, or AI that supports children with developmental differences that diagnose it earlier or support the provider in providing personalized treatment are the gold standard. As long as they are scientifically driven, those are great things. What gets closer to that ultraprocessed food, and concerns me, are AI companions. These plush toys are embedded with LLMs and are being marketed as a healthy alternative to screen time and your child’s first best friend, but that is uncharted territory, and I would hold off on that.</p><p><b>Consistent across all three of your books is that we have to extend caring about kids beyond our own home or neighborhood. There needs to be some sort of collective concern that this generation of kids could be raised in this way that could fundamentally rewire their brains. </b></p><p>You’re starting to see rumblings of this already, like people booing AI at commencements and pushing back on data centers. People are worried about their jobs, but I think it's actually something even more fundamentally basic: we don't want to be replaced in the roles that we play in each other's lives, as a partner, friend or parent. We could all be in our little, tiny Wall-E bubbles, but we don't want that.</p><p><b>It seems like the prevailing wisdom on AI is “well, it’s coming, and you’re not going to like it. Too bad.” Really? We can’t do anything? That helplessness rings false to me, and you write that ultimately, we can decide what to allow into our lives and our children’s lives.</b></p><p>We're at the beginning of this. We really are still much more in the driver's seat than we realize. We just have to realize it and act collectively. The one thing that is absolutely true is that we all love our kids more than anything. It defies any rationality, and it’s a great motivator. There’s nothing more human than that.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago small businesses hard hit by immigration raids eligible for $5,000 grants
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Hispanic Chamber of Commerce Foundation will award 52 grants of $5,000 each to qualifying Chicago-area small businesses affected by immigration raids and patrols.</p><p>Communities eligible in the first phase include<b> </b>Pilsen, Brighton Park, McKinley Park, Archer Heights, Back of the Yards, Little Village, Chicago Lawn, West Lawn, Berwyn and Cicero.</p><p>Grants will be distributed in three phases over a one-year period ending June 30, 2027.</p><p>“These grants will help local businesses stabilize, recover and continue serving as the economic backbone of their neighborhoods,” Jaime di Paulo, CEO of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/10/09/business-community-leaders-support-latino-il-hispanic-chamber-commerce-conference" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Hispanic Chamber of Commerce</u></a>, said in a news release on Thursday.</p><p>Applications open on Aug. 24 and close Sept. 14. Grant recipients will be announced on Oct. 1.</p><p>Businesses eligible for grants must have been running for at least two years, have 10 or fewer employees and have a valid business license, among other criteria.</p><p>Applicants must submit written statements limited to 250 words describing negative impacts on their business due to immigration enforcement actions, such as reduced revenue and operating hours, fewer customers, canceled events or other financial losses, IHCC Foundation said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure encourage people to support neighborhood businesses.</p><p>The Illinois Hispanic Chamber of Commerce launched its first “shop local” event in February in Brighton Park to promote small businesses in event because immigration raids had a major impact there. Foot traffic slowed dramatically along Archer Avenue’s commercial corridor.</p><p>Last October, U.S. Border Patrol agents in Brighton Park shot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" target="_blank" ><u>Marimar Martinez</u></a> five times. She survived, but the shooting sparked <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/04/shooting-involving-federal-agents-in-brighton-park-under-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>a confrontation</u></a> in the neighborhood between nearly 100 protesters and federal agents, some in an armed personnel carrier.</p><p>Last year, immigration agents often started their day in Brighton Park because there is a Home Depot nearby where laborers used to gather, said Hilda Alvarez Rodriguez, Illinois Hispanic Chamber of Commerce’s special projects manager, in February.</p><p>More than 78% of Brighton Park residents are Latino, according to the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning.</p><p>More information about the grants is at <a class="Link" href="http://ihccbusiness.net/resilientcommunitiesinitiative" target="_blank" ><u>ihccbusiness.net/resilientcommunitiesinitiative</u></a><u>.</u></p>

entries.title: Tom Grosspietsch, a well-known figure on Chicago's rollerblading scene, has died at 66
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p>Tom Grosspietsch was Chicago's shepherd on wheels. His flock — the Windy City Skaters, a group that came together nearly two decades ago to share a love for rollerblading, also known as inline skating.</p><p>Mr. Grosspietsch — pronounced like Gross Peach — collected his herd of several dozen riders under the gaze of the Picasso in Daley Plaza every other Friday during the warmer months to lead its most cherished ritual: Friday Night Road Raves.</p><p>After a quick rundown of the rules — helmets were a must, and there'd be no running of red lights — he blew a whistle, and the group began rolling through the Loop with the the sounds of tunes blaring from Bluetooth speakers affixed to backpacks.</p><p>The 13-mile route was known in advance only to Mr. Grosspietsch, who created themes for each journey. </p><p>His Great Chicago Fire ride, for instance, rolled past the the site of the fire's origin and included structures that survived the conflagration. He led a ride that went past spots associated with Democratic National Conventions and others that showcased locations seen in “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” and “The Blues Brothers." </p><p>His Pope Leo XIV ride went past the site of the Roman Catholic leader's birth, the South Side ballpark of his beloved White Sox and a Portillo's that named one of its beefs after the pontiff.</p><p>At each key spot, Mr. Grosspietsch blew his whistle, everyone stopped for a minute or two, Mr. Grosspietsch told a few interesting bits about the history connected to the spot, and then the party kept rolling.</p><p>He printed each map, which included photos and facts, handing them out after each ride.</p><p>Mr. Grosspietsch, who lived in Oak Park, died July 15 after being hospitalized in Chicago due to complications from blood cancer. He was 66.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-da0000" name="image-da0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"On every ride, he'd turn to me and say, 'So far, so good?'" said Kirsten Lefeldt, a civil engineer who added that Mr. Grosspietsch would skate the route ahead of time for quality assurance.</p><p>Windy City Skaters is planning a memorial ride later this summer. The theme will be Mr. Grosspietsch's life. Stops will include Grant Park, where he volunteered for years for the American Cancer Society's Walk and Roll fundraiser; Macy's on State Street, where Mr. Grosspietsch's work as an art director and graphic designer was displayed in windows for many years during the holiday season; and a place along the Near South Side lakefront where his skates left an imprint in concrete that was still wet.</p><p>Mr. Grosspietsch co-founded Windy City Skaters and was the driving force behind the group, which began hosting Friday night rides in 2008.</p><p>"He touched so many lives in such a positive way," said Nate Hill, 35, a software designer who lives in the West Loop and will help carry on Mr. Grosspietsch's legacy by leading future rides.</p><p>"When I moved here four years ago from Indiana, I didn't skate and was trying to figure out how to make friends," Hill said. "I learned about the meetup, and I practiced skating and went and checked it out. And it ended up changing my life in a huge way. I met so many amazing friends. and I've learned so much about Chicago. Tom's a legend in the community."</p><p>During the Friday night rides, you'll find Gerard Brouwer, 78, bringing up the rear, helping any stragglers and shouting "Stay the right!" to remind skaters to leave room for cars to pass.</p><p>"All of us were able to enjoy the benefits of Tom's hard work, and there's never been a charge or a fee for any of it," said Brouwer, who drives two hours from his home in LaSalle County to take part in the rides.</p><p>The group includes several people from Wisconsin and transplants from European and Asian countries where inline skating is more mainstream.</p><p>"It's a very inclusive group," Hill said. "The only through line is people who tend to prioritize their health. And Tom got purpose from bringing the community together. That's what he kind of lived for, in a way."</p><p>Mr. Grosspietsch was born Aug. 6, 1959, grew up in Barrington and loved playing hockey as a kid.</p><p>He was one of 12 siblings. One of them, Joseph, has since died.</p><p>His father John Grosspietsch died 1972, and Mr. Grosspietsch stepped in, along with his siblings, to help out his mother Margo Grosspietsch, family members said.</p><p>"He was a quiet shepherd back then, too," said Mr. Grosspietsch's brother Mike. "He'd pile us into the family station wagon — if it was running— and drive us to a public ice rink to skate and get us out of the house and give my mom a break."</p><p>Mr. Grosspietsch was once a competitive long-distance inline speedskater. He competed in events across the United States and Europe, mostly in his 40s.</p><p>He also hosted Skate Chicago, a free four-day event that invited skaters from around the country to take part in rides around the city.</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

entries.title: How Chicago helped a tiny Baltic country produce star NBA players
entries.summary: <p>VILNIUS, Lithuania — Arena Vilnius, half the size of the United Center, feels bigger than it is when hometown heroes Rytas play against the Žalgiris basketball team from Kaunas.</p><p>Sections of cheering fans wave giant flags and shout songs of adoration to their teams. Huge stationary flamethrowers send pillars of fire into the air, warming anyone within 20 yards.</p><p>When the underdogs Rytas briefly lead at the end of the third quarter, during a Sunday night game in April, the exuberance of the Rytas dance team makes it seem like they might get a win.</p><p>Domantas Purvys, a local high school basketball fanatic, volunteers at the arena to get free floor-level access to the games. He says basketball "is part of our religion. It's in our blood, basketball. It’s everything to us."</p><p>Like many Lithuanians, Purvys also follows the NBA.</p><p>"I love Matas Buzelis," he says of the rising <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> star, who's a cornerstone of the team's rebuilding plans.</p><p>Born in Chicago to Lithuanian immigrants, Buzelis, 21, is beloved in the country of 2.8 million people.</p><p>He's the latest accomplished basketball player with a Lithuanian name, along with Kasparas Jakučionis, who played for the University of Illinois before joining the Miami Heat and who's now with the Milwaukee Bucks, and Domantas Sabonis, the Sacramento Kings star who’s the son of Lithuanian giant Arvydas Sabonis, formerly of the Portland Trail Blazers.</p><p>Buzelis, Jakučionis and Jonas Valančiūnas, formerly of the Denver Nuggets, are playing in the off-season for the Lithuanian national team, which has an exhibition game Aug. 23 in Vilnius against the reigning NCAA champs University of Michigan.</p><div Chicago.</p><p>In the mid-1930s, Lithuania wanted to improve its basketball standing in Europe. So it invited diaspora Lithuanians to help.</p><p>Two Chicagoans, Juozas Žukas and Konstantinas Savickas, came to Kaunas to play for and coach the Lithuanian national team. They were joined by Frank Lubin, a Californian who'd played for the University of California Los Angeles and helped the U.S. win Olympic gold for basketball in 1936.</p><p>In 1937, the scrappy Lithuanian national team, featuring three Chicago players and a Chicago player-coach, Feliksas Kriaučiūnas, won the EuroBasket tournament.</p><p>Lithuania repeated its win in 1939, once again with four Chicago-area players.</p><p>"It dates back to guys from Chicago going there to play for the national team," Don Siliunas says. Siliunas is a radiologist who serves as president of the Lituanica Athletic Club at the Lithuanian World Center in Lemont, where Buzelis played in youth programs.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-440000" name="image-440000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/46b22c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6252x3509+0+331/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fd4%2Fe1449fad41eb94539c8d7aac5e25%2Flithuania-06xx26-136.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f923696/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6252x3509+0+331/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fd4%2Fe1449fad41eb94539c8d7aac5e25%2Flithuania-06xx26-136.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7f236ac/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6252x3509+0+331/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Fd4%2Fe1449fad41eb94539c8d7aac5e25%2Flithuania-06xx26-136.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mindaugas Balčiūnas, president of the Lithuanian Basketball Federation, stands in the lobby of the Lithuanian House of Basketball in Kaunas on April 16. "Chicago is one of the most important towns in the United States in terms of the Lithuanian community, in terms of help to Lithuanian basketball, and we really appreciate it."</p><p>During the half-century occupation of Lithuania by the former Soviet Union, Lithuanian players made up a disproportionate number of the Soviets' top players, including when four Lithuanian starters helped win a men's gold medal at the 1988 Summer Olympics.</p><p>Four years later, Lithuania was a newly independent country when it competed in the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona.</p><p>Underfunded and overshadowed by the American "Dream Team," featuring Michael Jordan, Larry Bird and Magic Johnson, the Lithuanians got help from an unexpected source: Members of the Grateful Dead saw a newspaper article about their plight and funded the team's trip to the Olympics.</p><p>American artist Greg Speirs designed yellow, green and red tie-dyed T-shirts with a dunking skeleton to fundraise for the team, attracting a worldwide spotlight to Lithuanian basketball. dunking skeletons are still a huge seller at the Lithuanian House of Basketball in Kaunas, Balčiūnas says. Even Denmark's king and queen wanted a shirt when they visited Lithuania in January, he says.</p><p>The 1992 Olympic bronze medal helped unify Lithuania, Balčiūnas says.</p><p>"The single voice of us as a nation and a country was basketball, just to announce to the world that look, we are independent. We have our country. We have our identity," he says.</p><p>As Lithuania's population declined from emigration, Balčiūnas says he's gotten creative to keep the sport and its recruiting efforts strong, especially because Lithuanian basketball receives significantly less funding from the International Basketball Federation than soccer gets from the International Federation of Association Football.</p><p>Balčiūnas and his staff look for promising youth players in the diaspora. He pulls out a 1911 baptismal certificate from a U.S. player's great-grandparent, proving their Lithuanian roots.</p><p>"We have competitors, nations with 100 million people, and we still need to beat them," Balčiūnas says. "That's why communities of immigrants are very, very important."</p><p>What Lithuania lacks in population, it makes up for in its reputation for strong preparation for the sport.</p><p>Nearly every town in the country, which is half the size of Illinois, has its own men's team. A handful also have a professional women's team.</p><p>Balčiūnas hopes interest in women's basketball will grow when Lithuania co-hosts the EuroBasket Women 2027 tournament.</p><p>Lithuanian coaches are legally required to have at least a bachelor's degree, and the country has several universities offering coaching studies.</p><p>"This is what we call our DNA of our basketball," he says. "People who are coming here, spending one or two years, they are starting to understand how basketball integrates in your brain, in your thinking, in your daily habits and so on."</p><p>Almantas Kiveris, press officer for the Žalgiris team, says Lithuania relied on American help in the beginning, but now it's become a two-way street.</p><p>"Even under full Soviet occupation, basketball was the leading sport, and every newborn was — we joke — born with a basketball in their hands," he says.</p><p>He points to Buzelis, playing for the Bulls and for Lithuania. "He was born in Chicago, but we still look at him as 100% Lithuanian.”</p><p>Žalgiris, the top team in Lithuania, routinely attracts former NBA players.</p><p>At a practice in April, several American players were running drills and scrimmaging, with an English-speaking assistant coach translating courtside.</p><p>At the Sanit Basketball Academy in Vilnius, 10- and 11-year-old boys are running drills on a weekday after school, each kid dribbling a basketball with his left hand while tossing and catching a little ball in his right.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Amid ‘wave of new Irish music,’ here are five acts from the Emerald Isle to catch at Lollapalooza
entries.summary: <p>Call it an Irish hello: A wide range of talent from the Emerald Isle will take center stage at Lollapalooza on the first day of the festival with five rising acts in the spotlight.</p><p>“There really is a wave of new Irish music coming through, but I think it’s seen across the board, even beyond music,” said Robbie Cunningham, singer/guitarist of the Dublin folk trio Amble, who play at 5:15 p.m. on the Airbnb Stage, breaking out in 2025 with the album “Reverie.” According to the band’s label, Warner Records, it was the biggest Irish album release since 2018.</p><p>“I think there’s a real moment in Ireland right now,” he said, referencing A-list actors like Jessie Buckley, Paul Mescal and Cillian Murphy, in addition to music bigwigs like Hozier and Fontaines D.C. “And I think it just takes one band or one person to go and do it for other people to follow [who] think, ‘I could do that, too.’ ”</p><p>Cunningham’s theory zeroes in on a phenomenon the Los Angeles Times<i> </i>has likened to a “Green Wave” and The Week<i> </i>has described as an insatiable hunger for Irish traditional music as of late, especially among younger listeners, even comparing the interest to modern-day Beatlemania. According to the Irish Recorded Music Association, the market share for Irish music has tripled since 2024, reaching 21.5% of the top 100 sales in 2025, driven by big releases from Hozier (a Lolla alum) as well as Amble, CMAT and Kingfishr (the latter two are also on the festival bill this year).</p><p>“When you look at someone like Hozier, he has had this crazy moment in the last five years, and he’s now bigger than anyone ever expected. And I find it interesting he’s taking other Irish bands on his tour with him in the United States. Does that correlate? I think it does,” said Avery Liardon, global festival talent buyer for Lollapalooza organizers C3 Presents. Notably, Amble opened several Hozier dates in America in 2025, including Fenway Park. Liardon also points to another relevant example of this sensation: when Chappell Roan, relatively unknown at the time, opened for Olivia Rodrigo a few months before playing in front of one of the biggest crowds ever recorded at Lollapalooza in 2024. “I think that might be the same Hozier/Amble effect of it all,” said Liardon. “Everything is one degree away from everything else.”</p><p>While the talent booker notes she and her team weren’t “consciously thinking about” booking Irish bands for the 2026 edition of the festival, you can't deny the team is thinking more internationally in recent years. Coupled with the fact that Lollapalooza now has six other international editions (Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Paris, India and Berlin), the festival has also seen wild success with the K-pop market and has the first Filipino band, SB19, taking the stage in Chicago this year.</p><p>Plus, as Liardon explains, there is a domino effect that affects the way acts are chosen for Lolla — a complicated web of working with agents, managers and other partners who have “thousands of bands to pitch” while they eye ongoing trends. As the profile of Irish bands continue to rise (Amble has the same team as Hozier), they become more covetable.</p><p>“When Amble comes over, they sell out all the rooms all over the U.S.,” she said. “So, we’re not just booking because we’re doing any favors … there's a real business here with a band like that.”</p><p>It’s an effect Amble taps into on its new single “The Swell,” which will be featured on an upcoming record in 2027 (expect some new material during their Lolla set). “It’s a song about us evolving and growing within the band, where you go from playing 300- to 400-cap rooms to then literally for 30,000 or 40,000 people. It’s an insane experience for the body and the mind,” said Amble instrumentalist/vocalist Oisín McCaffrey. He wrote the song and is looking forward to performing it in Chicago where many of his family live and will be in the crowd.</p><p>Remarkably, Amble only fully got together in 2024 with modest pub gigs; the band’s first show in Chicago was that fall at Schubas. At the time, McCaffrey worked as a data scientist for Pfizer and Cunningham and fellow bandmate Ross McNerney were teachers. All three have since quit their day jobs. “We all love playing the shows and we owe it to the crowd every night to give the best of ourselves,” he said. “That’s the message of ‘The Swell.’ It’s like a pinch me song, when you realize you are doing the coolest thing you could ever possibly do in your life.”</p><p>As Amble has found, young people in particular have been flocking to the band’s music, as recently seen at other fests like Bonnaroo. “I think it’s the authenticity that we're channeling out to the world,” McCaffrey said, speculating what’s behind the youth explosion for Irish music. “Every time people come to the shows, it’s just so real and there's nothing programmed. The gigs are such a huge singalong that it feels like a very communal experience, and I think people leave the shows feeling like they know each other in a way, too. It’s a beautiful thing.”</p><p><i>Here’s a look at the other Irish bands playing Lollapalooza, all on Thursday:</i></p><p><b>Kingfishr: </b>Irish trad music gets a modern eye with this Limerick trio who broke out with the 2025 album “Halcyon” (1:45 p.m., Tito’s Stage).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Chicago is at peak improv, with iO Fest and TJ & Dave returning
entries.summary: <p>Chicago is at peak improv at the moment.</p><p>This weekend marks<a class="Link" href="https://ioimprov.com/io-fest/" target="_blank" > the third annual iO Fest, </a>which is one of the biggest improv events in the world. Next weekend, improv legends <a class="Link" href="https://www.goodmantheatre.org/show/tj-dave-2026/" target="_blank" >TJ & Dave</a> perform at the Goodman Theatre. Then, in August, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.theatremomentum.com/festival" target="_blank" >Dramatic Improv Festival</a> arrives, heralding a unique brand of the artform. </p><p>So if it feels like improv is everywhere this summer, it is.</p><p>“When I first started, there weren't any real improv festivals,” said comedian TJ Jagodowski. He’s set to perform July 30 - Aug. 1 at the Goodman Theatre with his improv partner, David Pasquesi. As the duo TJ & Dave, the pair have been performing improv together for more than 24 years and are a familiar act to many Chicagoans.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>TJ Jagodowski (left) and David Pasquesi (right)</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Liz Lauren</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I think there were only two improv festivals in the whole country,” said Jagodowski. When he thought about the landscape of improv in the 1980s, he described Chicago as the center of the artform’s universe. “Basically, you trained in Chicago, and then went to New York. Or you trained in Chicago, and then an iO opened in Los Angeles. It was more centralized back then.”</p><p>Today, Jagodowski refers to Chicago as “the mecca of improv.” He said Chicago was the first city where you could see live improv seven nights a week. Over the years that reputation has held true. Bigger venues, like Second City, iO, and the Annoyance have enough shows to fill a weekly calendar.</p><p>But there are also smaller venues and companies, such as <a class="Link" href="https://logansquareimprov.com/" target="_blank" >Logan Square Improv,</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.bitimprov.org/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23874089188&gbraid=0AAAAA-EI0KuYO9NYKtGVn9iaVYAFXLSbr&gclid=Cj0KCQjw94bTBhDQARIsAN3vv0y4I7Xox0XmLNEFPiS65MTWrX6zJxSh6Ib_-ii1VDdXpIMGnl5Ec-MaAgyIEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >The Bit Theatre in Aurora</a>, or the weekly bilingual improv show, “<a class="Link" href="https://www.collaboraction.org/event-details/como-se-dice-a-bilingual-improv-comedy-show-2027-05-28-19-00" target="_blank" >¿Cómo se dice....?,</a>” hosted at Collaboraction’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/03/03/collaboraction-theatre-606-arts-corridor-chicago-stages-house-belonging" target="_blank" ><u>new theater,</u></a> called the House of Belonging, in Humboldt Park.</p><p>As for what it was about Chicago that has allowed improv to flourish, Pasquesi said the answer is in the long standing institutions like iO and the Second City, even if the latter leans more on sketch comedy than improv.</p><p>“When I was coming up, there was no other place that one with my skills could go, or acquire those skills,” he said. “It had to be physically in Chicago because you had to be in the same room back then, and this was the only place doing it.”</p><p>Jagodowski and Pasquesi perform the traditional brand of improv inspired by legendary Chicago comic <a class="Link" href="https://playbill.com/article/del-close-legendary-chicago-acting-and-improv-figure-dead-at-64-com-80458" target="_blank" ><u>Del Close.</u></a> If you visit iO Theatre, they are still performing the "Harold," which Close developed with iO cofounder Charna Halpern.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure </figure> </div> </div><p>Pasquesi studied with Close around the time the Harold was taking off. “I just happened to be in the room when all that was going on,” he said. “There would not be long form improvisation without him. He taught me more than I'll ever remember. And in addition to being a genius, he was a certifiable jagoff.”</p><p>A term commonly associated with this style of improv is “slow comedy.” But Jagodowski says the description doesn’t have anything to do with pacing of the performance. “It just means you're not going to sell out the relationship for perhaps a convenient joke,” he explained. “It keeps relationships at the center of everything you're trying to do, so where some improvisation is designed to be more entertaining, this is designed to maybe make you feel something or care.”</p><p>Relationships are of tremendous value to the duo, which has been performing together for over two decades.</p><p>“I'm not a big fan of repetition, rewatching things, or rereading or redoing,” said Pasquesi. “The really beautiful part of this is that 24 years into it, we've never done, and are never going to do, the same show twice. And that's sexy to me.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5d0000" Kobin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The weekend before TJ & Dave hit the stage at the Goodman, iO Fest is spinning the artform forward with its own slate of innovative acts, such as The Orbit, which embraces the “punk legacy” of performing in nontraditional spaces, said Gretchen Eng, performer, producer, and the director of education at iO Theatre.</p><p>“It is unlike anything else you'll see,” Eng said. “The performers sit around a round table in the middle of the room. And the audience sits in a concentric circle outside of them. In some of the most inventive physical comedy, as well as just artistic improv that we do, takes place because we don't have this like fourth wall convention as applied to this show.”</p><p>iO Fest’s 2026 lineup also includes Jackbox. Many people will recognize the name as the popular app-based multiplayer party game. At iO Fest, Jackbox will blend interactive party games with improv. </p><p>“The people who have devised the games and written for them have been plugged into the Chicago improv community for years and years,” said Eng.</p><p>A big shift in iO Fest this year, Eng said, is that programmers leaned into local talent as opposed to having famous outsiders be positioned as the big draw.</p><p>“I'm really excited for the bet we have made that our audience really wants to see not just these heavy hitters from out of town, but also the incredible groups that are already part of the Chicago Comedy network,” said Eng.</p><p>While Chicago talent is certainly the centerpiece, there are still big name headliners like The Sloppy Boys, a comedy rock band. They host a podcast of the same name, and formerly had a sketch comedy show on IFC called “The Birthday Boys,” produced by Bob Odenkirk.</p><p>Eng said Chicago remains a destination for aspiring improv performers around the world.</p><p>“People really do make it a lifelong dream to come and study improv in this city,” she said.</p>

entries.title: Chaotic, crowded Chicago immigration mega court hearings are fueling record deportation orders
entries.summary: <p>The benches in courtroom 11 at Chicago’s immigration court, the one judges lament as so tiny, barely seat 25.</p><p>So how could 143 people called for hearings on a single morning ever fit?</p><p>By 9:10 a.m., roughly 60 of them — mostly asylum seekers without lawyers — had crammed in wall-to-wall. Judge Peter Kim’s clerk squeezes through the waiting crowd this July morning to collect names and mark late arrivals present. The stakes are high: failing to show up to court could mean an automatic deportation order.</p><p>But the hearing itself is dense and complex, the judge’s litany of immigration jargon punctuated by crying children who are hungry and hot.</p><p>“You are here because the government believes that you should be removed,” Kim says through Creole and Spanish interpreters.</p><p>When he asks immigrants how many need more time to find an attorney, nearly every hand flies up.</p><p>Welcome to a “mega master” calendar hearing, a massive preliminary procedural hearing instituted by the Trump administration at the end of May that now crams between 100 and 185 people into a single judge’s morning’s call — as many as 70 into the same hearing if they don’t have lawyers. Not everyone shows up, but before May these hearings averaged 30 people. It’s not clear how the judges are chosen for these assignments.</p><p>Chicago, a large court with a large backlog, stands out with the most mega hearings in June in its courthouse at 55 E. Monroe, as well as the most scheduled at the same time, according to immigration scholar Austin Kocher. He pinpointed three mornings in June with mega hearings scheduled simultaneously before four judges — in addition to normal court business.</p><p>Anecdotally, July shows no signs of letting off the gas.</p><p>Attorneys and former judges say mega master hearings serve as the latest tool for the Trump administration to deport large numbers of people, this time by causing chaos and confusion in the courts. It’s a subtler tactic than last year’s headline-grabbing Operation Midway Blitz that hurt and killed immigrants and citizens. A spate of Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests inside courthouses already frightened immigrants from appearing.</p><p>Advocates say key purposes of mega hearings include discouraging immigrants from coming to court, smoothing the way toward deportation, and curtailing time to find an affordable attorney. When people miss court, judges can order them removed <i>in absentia</i> or in their absence.</p><p>In June, for the first time since 2019, more people were found to have missed court in Chicago than showed up, according to data released by the Executive Office of Immigration Review — immigration court’s formal name.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-cd0000" name="html-embed-module-cd0000"></a><div style="min-height:607px" id="datawrapper-vis-PU737"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/PU737/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-PU737"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/PU737/full.png" alt="More immigrants missed their Chicago court dates in June than appeared (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d90000" name="html-embed-module-d90000"></a><div style="min-height:510px" id="datawrapper-vis-fc1A9"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/fc1A9/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-fc1A9"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/fc1A9/full.png" alt="Nationally, most people still do appear in immigration court when summoned (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Of the 10,370 people assigned to hearings in June, 58% were ruled absent, according to EOIR data analyzed by Mobile Pathways, a nonprofit advocating for fair access and transparency in immigration proceedings.</p><p>Several other cities such as Dallas and Charlotte have already seen a greater number of <i>in absentia</i> rulings than immigrants present. Nationally, about 60% of immigrants called to court in June still showed up, down from 78% last October.</p><p>The amount of notice given to immigrants to come to court also has plummeted nationwide, but particularly in Chicago. Median lead time in June fell to just 34 days in Chicago, down from 229 days in May, according to data analyzed by BKLG, another non-profit that examines federal immigration data.</p><p>The U.S. Justice Department oversees immigration court, and officials there say that the amped-up scheduling is meant to clear backlogs that has left immigrants on dockets for years awaiting a decision on whether they made a case to stay or not.</p><p>Asked for an interview, an EOIR spokesperson shared a prepared statement that said it “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases, including those of unaccompanied alien children, and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish,” the statement reads. “As it continues to add new immigration judges, EOIR will continue to make scheduling adjustments to ensure all cases are handled in a timely and lawful manner.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure fail to show up for hearings another “tactic to facilitate deportations.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Stephanie Spiro, an attorney with the National immigration Justice Center, calls the recent surge of <i>in absentia</i> removal orders “unprecedented.”</p><p>“It’s not a coincidence, but another tactic to facilitate deportations,” she says.</p><p>The mega hearings aren’t about speeding up cases but about eliminating them for people who don’t show up, Spiro says: “It's much more efficient for the government to deport people without even having to read any briefs, without having to have a full hearing, without having to schedule hundreds of people, and actually listen to their claims, and afford them due process.”</p><p>The court counts “on the fact that they're not going to get notice, and even if they do … they're not going to go, because they're afraid of being deported and separated from their families and children.”</p><p>That fear had Carolina, an immigrant from Venezuela who just gave birth here, debating whether to go to her hearing on Thursday.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ are not using her full name because she’s afraid it could jeopardize her asylum application.</p><p>Without a lawyer, she worries her family could be ordered arrested and deported during their court appointment. She fears one of her kids could get deported to Peru, where she was born.</p><p>“And I don't have family in Peru,” she says. “I don't want to get separated from my family, or get separated from my newborn. At least this month he will get his passport."</p><p>In the end, Carolina and her husband brought the children to court. In a lucky break, they were given more time for their case. But she had prepared for the worst, saying, “I was terrified.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" She had no new job lined up.</p><p>“Whenever you have a high volume of anything in any field, it leaves a possibility for error because of fatigue [and] because of the repetitive nature of what you're reviewing,” says Treacy. “I never wanted to make a mistake in those kinds of circumstances.”</p><p>Treacy says at these large hearings, indigenous applicants — who are from Ecuador and Guatemala and aren’t fully fluent in Spanish — are less likely to report critical language barriers.</p><p>“It's an intimidating atmosphere for somebody to raise their hand and say, ‘I'm sorry, I don't fully understand what you're saying,’” Treacy says.</p><p>She and other former judges also noted that <i>in absentia </i>deportation orders require a meticulous, review of government records and hearing notices that can’t be rushed.
