the pressure of the mega master hearings, free and low cost legal help has long waiting lists.</p><p>And without an attorney, even something as simple as changing an address can present a hurdle.</p><p>None of the 70-plus immigrants sharing a single mega master hearing before Judge Marc Stahl in courtroom 7 have a lawyer.</p><p>Stahl fills every seat, including the chairs in front of enough.</p><p>“Do you understand these rights?” he asks. “Raise your hand and keep it raised.”</p><p>Stahl flags another particularity of immigration court: The burden of proof in pleading a case to stay in the U.S. is on the immigrant, not the government.</p><p>“Please listen carefully,” Stahl tells them, spelling out the new realities of immigration court under the Trump administration.<b>   </b></p><p>“If you fail to appear at a court date,” he says, “you will be ordered removed <i>in absentia</i>.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Keenan Chen</i></p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: At Joliet prison, desperate men set themselves on fire
entries.summary: <p>Around 10 p.m., a haze of gray smoke wafted down a hallway lined with prison cells at the Joliet Treatment Center. The window of cell A9 began to glow red as the fire within grew. Jason Stephens was locked inside. Minutes ticked by, and the smoke became so thick you could not see more than a few feet. No one came to let Stephens out.</p><p>There have been more than 70 fires at the facility in the last three years, according to an investigation by The Marshall Project, WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times. That includes a dozen cases in which men incarcerated there set themselves on fire.</p><p>The Joliet Treatment Center opened in 2017 with the promise of being a new kind of prison in Illinois, designed to provide intensive mental health treatment. But in the years leading up to that night in the summer of 2024, incarcerated men and civil rights lawyers who visited the facility said the conditions declined. Men were kept locked in their cells for long stretches, with nothing to do. They complained about a lack of medical care and mental health treatment, which the prison system is legally obligated to provide. Men reported that guards used excessive force.</p><p>As the men grew more despondent, some became willing to do anything to draw attention to their troubles and resorted to setting their cells — or themselves — on fire.</p><p>One man needed surgery to graft new skin onto his charred calf.</p><p>Another lost a leg.</p><p>Two have died.</p><p>Last year, the prison — with a population of about 200 people — recorded roughly three fires a month.</p><p>Despite that, officials at the Joliet Treatment Center have repeatedly failed to meet their responsibilities to prevent or respond to the fires, government records show.</p><p>Cellblocks lacked sprinklers, and fire alarms were turned off or inoperable. At an annual inspection, the prison would not provide a fire evacuation plan. Guards delayed ambulances responding to emergencies at the prison or trying to take men with serious injuries to the hospital.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Corrections did not answer questions about the epidemic of fires at Joliet Treatment Center, but in an email a spokesperson wrote that it is “committed to ensuring the safety and security of staff, individuals in custody, and all persons who enter our facilities” and takes its responsibility to uphold requirements related to facility safety seriously.</p><p>Craig Haney, a professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz and an expert on mental health in prisons, said the frequency of fires at the Joliet Treatment Center is a sign of abject hopelessness.</p><p>“These are the kinds of desperate acts that somebody takes when they feel they have no alternative,” Haney said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Allen Cunningham / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A disastrous delay</h3><p>As the blaze in Stephens’ cell intensified, three correctional officers gathered around a desk in a nearby room. Security camera footage from that night on July 27, 2024, shows that they seemed to notice something was wrong on the wing and grabbed a fire extinguisher. A call for help went out over the prison radio, and more officers slowly trickled in and put on medical gloves and masks.</p><p>About 10 minutes after smoke began to seep out of Stephens’ cell, officers entered the hallway.</p><p>Guards sprayed a fire extinguisher and pepper spray into his cell through a slot in the door usually used to deliver food.</p><p>Then, with Stephens still locked inside, they walked away.</p><p>A prison worker called 911. The fire department arrived within minutes, but precious time had already been lost. And more was about to be wasted.</p><p>Corrections officers told firefighters that the fire was out and that they needed help to clear out the smoke. According to a fire department incident report, it wasn’t until later, as the firefighters set up fans and officers meandered nearby, that prison employees mentioned that someone was still locked inside the burnt cell.</p><p>A group of guards and firefighters opened Stephens’ door, stained black with soot. Firefighters found Stephens lying on the floor, unconscious but still breathing, after having spent a half hour in a smoke-filled cell.</p><p>They looked into his airway and found it charred. Guards handcuffed his unconscious body, and he was loaded into an ambulance waiting outside.</p><p>But at the prison’s exit, guards refused to open the gate for the ambulance to leave until prison employees filled out paperwork and guards were ready to follow in a van.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>An argument erupted, and a guard walked up to the ambulance, yanking open the driver’s door. A group of firefighters and guards rushed over to intervene.</p><p>According to one guard, a firefighter said, “This man can die while y’all pussyfooting around.”</p><p>As the guards and firefighters argued with each other, one guard pulled another away, attempting to defuse the tension.</p><p>But the prison still would not allow the ambulance to depart.</p><p>A firefighter called his dispatcher again and again to report that the ambulance was stuck, with Stephens in the back hooked up to a machine forcing air into his lungs. Guards made the ambulance wait for nearly 28 minutes before finally opening the gate, allowing it to drive to a nearby hospital.</p><p>The next day, Stephens was moved to a Chicago-area hospital. Doctors performed a tracheotomy, cutting a hole in his throat so they could insert a breathing tube. But they could not save him.</p><p>Two weeks later, at age 38, Jason Stephens died. The medical examiner listed his official cause of death as “complications of inhalational injuries due to mattress fire.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cd0000" name="image-cd0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77dde3f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1821a70/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f878626/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Patrice Daniels at the Dixon Correctional Center, where he's currently incarcerated. Daniels says he saw firsthand the decline of Joliet Treatment Center — from a productive and healing environment to a more punitive and locked-down facility." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f878626/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/07f5e37/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f878626/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fae%2F1148cb7e49ca853123cc365d5c94%2Fprisonfires-260726-11.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Patrice Daniels at the Dixon Correctional Center, where he’s currently incarcerated. Daniels says he saw firsthand the decline of Joliet Treatment Center — from a productive and healing environment to a more punitive and locked-down facility.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times<br></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A hope betrayed </h3><p>Patrice Daniels sifted through a gray box of Stephens’ belongings. While incarcerated at the prison, Daniels’ job was to pack up the property of men who transferred out or died.</p><p>For Daniels, the fires — and the hopelessness that led men to set them — felt especially tragic because the Joliet Treatment Center was supposed to be a model of a prison that prioritized mental health treatment and healing, instead of punishment.</p><p>As a child, Daniels survived sexual abuse and would injure himself by banging his head on the wall. In his teens, he was in and out of mental hospitals and juvenile detention, where he put glass in his ears and eyes. At 18, he killed a woman in a park. He turned himself into police and confessed and was sentenced to life in prison for murder. He continued to mutilate himself. Instead of receiving therapy, he said, he was put in solitary confinement for stealing razor blades that he had cut himself with.</p><p>Sometimes, he said officers tied down his limbs and injected him with psychotropic drugs.</p><p>More than a decade after Daniels landed in prison, a lawyer asked him to join a lawsuit accusing the Illinois Department of Corrections of failing to treat the mental illnesses of people in the state’s prisons.</p><p>After a yearslong battle, the Department of Corrections settled the case and committed to opening a facility dedicated to providing mental healthcare: the Joliet Treatment Center. Daniels called it the most gratifying day of his life.</p><p>In 2017, Daniels was among the first people transferred to the new prison in what had been a juvenile detention center. The building smelled clean, nothing like the overwhelming scent of mold and feces he was used to in other prisons. The officers played cards and basketball with the men. Therapy and psychiatry were readily available.</p><p>In the first two years of the Joliet Treatment Center, a court-appointed monitor reported that men there routinely had plenty of time outside their cells and received 15 hours of structured therapeutic activity a week, unlike in some other prisons. But then, the once-hopeful mood dimmed.</p><p>A new warden took over in early 2020. According to Daniels, she had a more punitive approach. Daniels said the start of COVID-19 that year gave the prison an excuse to keep men isolated in their cells for long stretches with little treatment, and the facility never rebounded.Over the next few years, the prison began to cancel mental health groups and recreational time. Men complained about frequent use of pepper spray.</p><p>Daniels said that in the early years of the Joliet Treatment Center he’d allowed himself to become emotionally vulnerable. He felt betrayed by the prison’s new harshness.</p><h3>Fires as a way to be heard</h3><p>A mental health worker at the prison said she noticed men hurting themselves more frequently when the coronavirus lockdowns began. Prison employees got numb to the routine self-harm.</p><p>They “experienced something that the human brain was not meant to process,” said the worker, who asked not to be named because she still works in corrections and fears retaliation for talking about the conditions she saw at the Joliet Treatment Center.</p><p>“In order to do our job every day, we had to expect it,” she said, “and we had to get used to it.”</p><p>Around the same time, men began to set fires.</p><p>The Marshall Project interviewed or corresponded with seven men and asked why they set their cells, or themselves, on fire at the Joliet Treatment Center. They described poor medical treatment, and loneliness while being locked in their cells.</p><p>Many said that prison employees had grown inured to other forms of self-harm. But fires were impossible to ignore.</p><p>“We try to talk and write to them, but they don’t respect that. But when we act like animals and set things on fire and ourselves on fire, they listen,” one man said.</p><p>In the spring of 2020, Alexander Yracheta set himself on fire, after he said the prison repeatedly canceled his mental health groups, and he spent much of his time alone in his cell. He used the spark from an electrical outlet to light a cloth tied to his leg.</p><p>According to prison investigations, guards pulled him from the cell and put cuffs on his legs while his shorts were still on fire. He later had to have skin graft surgeries to repair the damage to his leg. The pain had been excruciating, but he said it was worth it to go to the hospital and get a break from his cell.</p><p>“I couldn’t really take it,” he said, adding, “I knew I had to do something extreme to get out.”</p><h3>“A really busy shift”</h3><p>No one knows for sure what made Stephens start the fire in his cell. But examining his path to that day in 2024 offers some clues.</p><p>Stephens had a difficult life, according to his family and court records. As a toddler, he was diagnosed with sickle cell disease, a genetic disorder that can cause blood cells to become misshapen, leading to episodes of extreme pain and organ damage. Sometimes, his muscles hurt so badly he couldn’t move and would just scream.</p><p>Around age 7, he and his mother were living on the street and in shelters. By 14, he had dropped out of school and would pick up odd jobs in construction. Stephens’ medical records say he began struggling with mental illness as a child and was eventually diagnosed with major depressive disorder, with psychotic features and PTSD.</p><div class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>When Stephens was 27 years old, he was arrested and charged with shooting a friend in a drug dispute a few years before. Stephens maintained his innocence. Court records note he had been hearing voices, but a judge found him mentally fit to stand trial. In 2015, a jury found him guilty of murder, and he was sentenced to 50 years in prison.</p><p>Behind bars, Stephens routinely complained to guards, nurses and doctors about extreme pain from his sickle cell disease.</p><p>Dr. William Weber, a physician and medical director at the Medical Justice Alliance, an organization dedicated to ensuring that people in prison get proper healthcare, reviewed Stephens’ medical records for The Marshall Project. Weber said the records show that when the prison took him to outside hospitals, doctors prescribed Stephens with medications for sickle cell pain, but the prison often failed to provide them to him.</p><p>By early 2024, housed at a maximum-security prison, Stephens made more desperate pleas for attention. He staged a hunger strike that lasted for 34 days. When that failed to get him the medical help he wanted, he asked employees, “What do I need to do to get medical treatment or sent to the hospital? Cut myself or swallow a bunch of pills?”</p><p>Later that day, he swallowed two razor blades and a nail clipper. The prison system refused to send him to the hospital because the facility was on lockdown due to a staffing shortage.</p><p>His medical records note several hospital visits in the ensuing weeks, but it’s unclear when, or if, those objects were ever removed.</p><p>Prison officials transferred Stephens to the Joliet Treatment Center in May 2024, presumably to give him additional mental health help. Stephen’s mental health records show some psychiatric visits, but rarely mention indivdual therapy and largely reflect brief mental health evaluations conducted to assess his risk of suicide.</p><p>At the Joliet Treatment Center, Stephens continued to complain about the lack of medical treatment. He insisted he needed a specific kind of blood transfusion that had helped him in the past. A prison doctor acknowledged that he would have “been better off” with the transfusion but failed to make sure he got the treatment.</p><p>In early July 2024, an officer at the Joliet Treatment Center wrote in a report that Stephens said he was going to do whatever he needed to do to get medical help, including hurting himself. “This has been an ongoing issue,” the officer wrote.</p><p>One day, a few weeks later, several men on Stephens’ wing began to harm themselves. Two of the men were sent to a separate part of the prison, and guards tied down their arms and legs in what are called four-point restraints. A doctor sent a third man to the emergency room.</p><p>The mental health worker, who was also on duty that day, said even with all the chaos, it was a normal day at the Joliet Treatment Center.</p><p>“It’s just what we would call a really busy shift,” she said.</p><p>By the end of the day, Stephens was one of only two men remaining on the wing. The other man said later that they both told officers they were also in crisis and wanted help. But no one from the mental health team responded.</p><p>That night, Stephens set a fire in his cell.</p><h3><b>A lack of fire preparedness</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Corrections did not answer questions about the fire in Stephens’ cell or about his complaints about medical care, citing pending litigation. The department has refused to provide a full investigative report about the incident, and The Marshall Project has sued to obtain the record, along with those of other fires. The lawsuits remain ongoing.</p><p>Still, there is evidence the Joliet Treatment Center was unprepared for the fire that killed Stephens, even after more than a dozen earlier blazes at the prison.</p><p>In an interview with prison investigators, an electrician at the facility said that the wing where Stephens was housed didn’t have working alarms or sprinklers. The only safety plan, he said, was for “correctional staff to be vigilant to watch for fires.” He said the issue was raised in staff meetings prior to Stephens’ death, but the fire protection systems never got fixed.</p><p>The Illinois State Fire Marshal’s Office, which inspects buildings to ensure that they meet fire codes, repeatedly documented problems at the prison. In 2023, a year before Stephens’ death, a fire marshal noted alarms in other parts of the prison were disconnected or inoperable and that prison employees said they said they didn’t know if the alarms worked on the wing where Stephens would later set the fire. The prison also couldn’t produce a written plan for how to evacuate the building. Days before Stephens set his fire, a marshal again noted similar violations.</p><p>As far back as 2020, local fire officials had complained that guards delayed ambulances trying to enter and exit the prison grounds to respond to fires. Jeff Carey, chief of the Joliet Fire Department, said that his department reached out several times to the prison’s administrators before Stephens’ death to get the problem fixed, to no avail.</p><h3>“Treatment doesn’t happen there”</h3><p>In the years since Stephens’ death, the fires have persisted unabated at the Joliet Treatment Center. There have been more than 60 since then, including at least eight cases of self-immolation, according to department records.</p><p>In November 2024, officers saw flames coming from under the cell door of a man named Latrell Edwards. They evacuated other men housed on his wing before letting him out of his cell, according to prison reports. Edwards was taken to the hospital with labored breathing and soot coating his throat and died two months later.</p><p>Since Stephens’ death, fire officials have continued to note delays at the gate and problems with alarms and evacuation plans.</p><p>The mental health worker at the Joliet Treatment Center said that prison employees had grown used to the fires, even after two men had died. That made it easier to ignore problems. “It's almost like there’s nothing they can do that will shock us anymore,” she said, adding, “No matter what they do, it’s not enough.”</p><p>As the prison environment became more focused on security and punishment, and opportunities to provide meaningful therapy declined, she decided to leave.</p><p>Daniels said that for a long time he had hoped he could help the prison return it to its mission of healing. But the culture became so toxic that last year he asked the Illinois Department of Corrections to transfer him to another prison.</p><p>As he rode away in a prison van, his legs and hands shackled, he saw the sign for the Joliet Treatment Center, and he thought, “That’s a sham. Treatment doesn’t happen there.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-420000" entries.title: Bears' Caleb Williams makes debut on 'NFL Top 100' list ahead of several star quarterbacks
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>’ popularity has been climbing all offseason, and Friday he made his debut on the NFL Top 100 list at No. 51. The rankings are determined by player voting and released incrementally over several months leading up to the season.</p><p>Williams did not make the list going into either of his first two seasons, but took a step forward last season by setting the Bears’ franchise record with 3,942 yards and pulling off seven fourth-quarter comebacks, including a playoff win.</p><p>At quarterback, that puts Williams ahead of former Eagles Super Bowl MVP Jalen Hurts (No. 56), fellow 2024 first-round pick Bo Nix of the Broncos (No. 59), the Jaguars’ Trevor Lawrence (No. 62), Ravens two-time MVP Lamar Jackson (No. 69), the Packers’ Jordan Love (No. 72), the Buccaneers’ Baker Mayfield (No. 77), the 49ers’ Brock Purdy (No. 85) and the Panthers’ Bryce Young (No. 98).</p><p>Williams and Young will face each other in Week 1 when the Bears visit the Panthers on Sept. 13.</p><p>Defensive end Montez Sweat is the only other Bear revealed to be in the Top 100 so far at No. 91. The league will unveil two players each day next week starting with Nos. 49 and 50 on Monday.</p>

Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuiyhn-l-t/" target="_blank" >Chaotic, crowded Chicago immigration mega court hearings fuel record deportation orders</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuiyhn-l-i/" target="_blank" >Adriana Cardona-Maguigad</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuiyhn-l-d/" target="_blank" >Lauren FitzPatrick</a></h5><p><b>'Mega' hearings</b>: At a "mega master" calendar hearing, a massive preliminary procedure instituted by the Trump administration at the end of May, between 100 and 185 people cram into a single immigration judge's morning call — and as many as 70 into the same hearing if they don't have lawyers. Not everyone shows up, but before May, these hearings averaged 30 people. It's not clear how judges are chosen for these assignments.</p><p><b>Chicago spike</b>: Chicago, a large court with a large backlog, stands out with the most mega hearings in June in its courthouse at 55 E. Monroe, and with the most scheduled at the same time, according to immigration scholar Austin Kocher. He pinpointed three mornings in June with hearings scheduled simultaneously before four judges, in addition to normal court business. Anecdotally, July has shown no signs of letting off the gas.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Attorneys and ex-judges say mega master hearings are the latest tool for the Trump administration to deport large numbers of people, this time by causing chaos and confusion in the courts. Advocates say a key purpose is to discourage immigrants from coming to court, smoothing the way toward deportation. It's a subtler tactic than last year’s headline-grabbing Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p><b>Recent day in court</b>: The benches in courtroom 11, which judges lament as so tiny, barely seat 25. So how could 143 people called for hearings on a July morning fit? By 9:10 a.m., roughly 60 people — mostly asylum seekers without lawyers — had crammed in wall-to-wall. A clerk squeezed through the crowd to collect names and mark late arrivals present. But a couple of years ago, Vann began working at Fillmore Linen Service, a commercial laundry in North Lawndale serving the healthcare industry. De Koven St. The girls learned about fire safety, participated in drills and spent time with members of the CFD.</p><p>"I consider them very important heroes," Hannah said. </p><p>The girls came from across the city. Other attendees were from CFD’s Camp Courage.</p><p>At the event, participants were able to try on bunker gear, run through obstacle courses, practice CPR on dummies and spray water from a firehose. entries.title: Obama drops in at WNBA event inspiring ninth grade girls at presidential center
entries.summary: <p>Fourteen-year-old London Harris has dreams of someday being president of the United States, and on Friday morning she got to see a former commander-in-chief up close. </p><p>Former President Barack Obama surprised London, along with nearly 100 other ninth grade girls during the third annual WNBA Changemaker Day at the recently opened Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>"It felt very surreal," said London, a student at Dyett High School in Washington Park. "I was genuinely happy to see him and to listen to what he had to say." </p><p>Obama popped into the center's Elie Wiesel Auditorium just as a panel of speakers was discussing the power of perseverance.</p><p>“I know you’re all learning the power of perseverance, the power of resilience, the power of dreaming big and this person," WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told the crowd. "No one has inspired hundreds of millions of people around the world here in the United States.” </p><p>Obama then walked on stage to thunderous applause.</p><p> “Hello, everybody!” Obama exclaimed, wearing jeans and a white button-down shirt.</p><p>“Settle down now,” he said, smiling, as the crowd screamed.</p><p>“I wasn’t gonna let a bunch of amazing young athletes, scholars, hoopers, come through my spot without saying hello," he said. "I’m not gonna start shaking hands yet because mayhem will break loose."</p><p>He began by telling the girls how proud he was of them and then spoke of his own experiences of being a dad to two daughters.</p><p>“Malia is now 28, Sasha is 25, but I remember like it was yesterday when they were your age,” Obama said. “We live in a world that is a lot more complicated for you guys than it was in some ways when I was coming up. There’s so much pressure and noise, and sometimes I think — especially for girls and young women — there’s social attitudes that tell you that you need to be one kind of way.”</p><div aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>He then encouraged the girls that they were on the right track.</p><p>“You are going to do wonderful things, and you need to have the confidence and power that’s inside you and your capacity to, you know, live out your dreams. ... You’re gonna have to work hard, and it’s not going to be easy, but I’m confident it’s gonna happen.”</p><p>Obama joked with the girls about boys being “knuckleheads” and urged them to seek guidance from others.</p><p>“One of the most important things you can do as a young person is find people who are willing to help you,” Obama said.</p><p>"Find mentors. Find people who are doing the kinds of things you want to do and learn from them," he added. "We only see the little fishbowl that we live in, but you know, it turns out there’s a whole big world out there full of possibilities. ... The more you see out there that’s possible, the better off you’re going to be.”</p><p>Obama then joked about talking too long because he spots one of the girls “about to fall asleep.”</p><p>“I’m used to it. That’s what it’s like at the Obama dinner table,” he said.</p><p>Obama shook hands with some of the girls as they screamed, then took a selfie with the crowd before leaving the stage.</p><p>Aliyah Myles, a student at Chicago Vocational Career Academy, grew up with Obama being a constant presence in her household. She described the former president as a huge influential figure for her mother. </p><p>Next time Aliyah talks to her mother, she'll get to tell her she shook Obama's hand. </p><p>"I was freaking out, I was turnt, I almost passed out," Aliyah, 14, said. "I was everywhere." </p><p>The event kicked off just before 10 a.m. with comments from WNBA brand strategist Nina Kossoff. Friday's gathering was among many events in Chicago this week tied to the WNBA All-Star Game, which will be held Saturday at the United Center.</p><p>“We’re powerful on our own, but when we come together, we can really make change,” Kossoff told the girls.</p><p>They also heard from a panel featuring Ari Chambers, an ESPN Journalist and commentator; Kizmet Mills, chief diversity officer at Nike; Linnae Harper, a former Chicago Sky player and now manager of athletics and sports leadership for the Obama Foundation; and Colie Edison, the WNBA's chief growth officer.</p><p>It was the third WNBA Changemaker Day, and this year's theme was "Finding My Superpower" — something each panelist touched on.</p><p>When I think about the word 'superpower,’ the first thing that comes to mind is doing the impossible,” Harper said. “My personal superpower is connecting people with their resources, providing a pathway for them to reach their goals.” </p><p>Others on the panel spoke on helping others through basketball, leadership and community efforts. The panelists then dived into explaining how they bounced back from their setbacks.</p><p>The students had begun trickling into the auditorium around 9:30 a.m. Some of the girls conversed and laughed while they waited, while others danced in their seats to Justin Timberlake’s “Can’t Stop the Feeling.” </p><p>In addition to Obama's surprise appearance, students were inspired by the panelists to continue pursuing their dreams and rise through any adversity they face. </p><p>"This really inspired me to keep going, push everything, take time, be patient and just focus on my dreams and career," said RaKaila Jefferson, 14. </p><p>For Aliyah, the event reinforced her aspirations to want to make an impact wherever she can. </p><p>"My goal is to make a change," Aliyah said. "I want to be known somewhere around the world." <br></p>

entries.title: 60 songs we’re listening to ahead of Lollapalooza 2026
entries.summary: <p>Lollapalooza starts on July 30. Whether you’re planning to be in the throng or settled comfortably on your couch, the festival often taps aspiring acts that go on to bigger things.</p><p>The festival’s headliners are stacked this year, drawing thousands to Grant Park for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/09/20/review-lorde-ultrasound-tour-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Lorde</u></a>, John Summit, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/04/29/chicago-charli-xcx-concert-allstate-arena-review-brat-pack" target="_blank" ><u>Charli XCX</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/11/18/billy-corgan-smashing-pumpkins-night-of-mellon-collie-infinite-sadness-lyric-opera" target="_blank" ><u>The Smashing Pumpkins</u></a>, Olivia Dean, JENNIE, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/08/16/tate-mcrae-builds-a-concert-on-familiar-moves" target="_blank" ><u>Tate McRae</u></a> and The XX. But the big names are joined by more than 100 other artists, and it’s easy to get lost in the sea of text when checking out each day’s schedule.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe style="border-radius: 12px" width="100%" height="352" title="Spotify Embed: Vocalo's Lollapalooza Guide" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen allow="autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; fullscreen; picture-in-picture" loading="lazy" src="https://open.spotify.com/embed/playlist/3KM2UJNEqmQsOJJkRMmKEV?si=9d763ea2a1094620&utm_source=oembed"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Consider Vocalo’s 2026 Lollapalooza playlist your festival survival guide, narrowing down some of the artists from the staggering lineup. The aim is to introduce you to talent taking stage earlier in the day, including Latin soul and indie rock influenced singer <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hODsGN-SjDw" target="_blank" ><u>54 Ultra</u></a>, pop-R&B artist Justine Skye, high school riot grrrl rock band Kim Theory, jazz-R&B musician Destin Conrad and Irish country singer CMAT.</p><p>Chicago talent also is featured on the stages and our playlist: Friday’s Chicago Made showcase includes viral “Top of Cars” rapper Lil M.U., R&B newcomer Sherrionn, rock band Free Joel and Grammy-winning artist-slash-producer <a class="Link" href="https://vocalo.org/petter-cottontale-interview-bekoe" target="_blank" ><u>Peter CottonTale</u></a>, while local experimental rock duo Water From Your Eyes and alt-country band <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/08/22/case-oats-last-missouri-exit-album-casey-gomez-walker" target="_blank" ><u>Case Oats</u></a> are set to perform on Saturday.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.lollapalooza.com/schedule" target="_blank" ><u>Find the full schedule</u></a> on Lollapalooza’s website, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/vocalo/" target="_blank" ><u>follow along</u></a> with Vocalo’s festival coverage on Instagram.</p>
entries.author: Morgan Ciocca | Vocalo

entries.title: Chicago murals: John Prine painting adorns Old Town School of Folk Music
entries.summary: <p>For John Prine fans, the massive new mural painted on the Old Town School of Folk Music in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lincoln-square" >Lincoln Square</a> can prompt pedestrians to stop and blink back tears.</p><p>The Maywood native and folk music legend <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/4/7/21199609/john-prine-dead-folksinger-songwriter-hello-in-there" >died in 2020 from COVID complications</a>. This month, his friend and fellow musician Jon Langford, who designed the mural, teamed up with Chicago artist Darius Dennis, owner of Big Wall Sign & Mural, to paint a tribute to Prine on the school’s second story brick wall during its annual Square Roots Festival. Prine once took lessons there in the 1960s and remained a mainstay as his career took off.</p><p>“It’s our thing,” Dennis says of big mural projects. His company has painted giant, lifelike murals for major advertisers like Porsche and Oscar Mayer and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics/2024/11/15/chicago-murals-darius-dennis-cta-red-line-civil-rights-danny-lyon-toddle-house-uptown" >Civil Rights-era photo reproduction murals in Uptown and Wicker Park</a>. A giant mural commemorating one of Chicago’s — and the world’s — most beloved folk singers? No problem.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-640001" name="image-640001"></a> <picture It features an older Prine strumming his guitar in front of a Chicago-flag blue background with red Chicago stars. His song lyrics, “How lucky can one man get?” stretch in a wavy line above him.</p><p>In white are tributes to Prine’s life, much of it referencing his job as a mail carrier before his musical career took off. “Maywood, Illinois,” his hometown, is written in postcard lettering on the left side of the mural. The postcard appears to be flipped on the right side and features Prine’s signature and two stamps with the face of his old friend and fellow Chicago musician, Steve Goodman. While Goodman was not a mail carrier, a Lake View post office is named after him.</p><p>A pennant honors Proviso East High School, Prine’s alma mater. entries.title: All-Star Angel Reese sky-high and living the Dream; says double-doubles 'don't matter' without winning
entries.summary: <p>No way Angel Reese was going to miss a chance to capture a moment Friday with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/24/obama-wnba-all-star-game-changemaker" target="_blank" >former President Barack Obama</a>, who dropped in on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" target="_blank" >WNBA</a>’s All-Stars before their media duties got underway at the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>“Gotta get your pic,” Reese said. “Not everybody’s going to meet Barack.”</p><p>The truth is Reese, the former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> firebrand now playing in Atlanta, vibed even more with former first lady Michelle Obama, on whose podcast she appeared as a guest in April.</p><p>“She made me feel the empowerment of what [being] a woman is like, to go through so many different things, to be in front of the world and have your back against the wall and go against the odds [with] everything she was doing. She gave me a lot of advice, so I appreciate Michelle. She poured so much into me, and I’m just really happy.”</p><p>Reese wasn’t always thrilled with things in Chicago, where the Sky went 13-27 and 10-34 in her two seasons. She lost and lost, occasionally did battle with the media, dealt with slings and arrows from abusive fans and eventually soured on the organization that drafted her No. 7 overall in 2024.</p><p>It’s so much better with the Dream, who entered the All-Star break in excellent shape at 16-10, including a 2-0 mark against Reese’s old team.</p><p>“They welcomed me with open arms,” Reese said. “It feels like a really safe place for me. It’s the safest I’ve ever felt, the most loved I’ve ever felt and I’m just really happy.</p><p>“They made me feel loved from the beginning. There’s nothing I can’t ask for. When I come to practice, it just feels like basketball. I don’t think about anything else. Starbucks is waiting in your locker. Anything I need, I got it. I ain’t never had that before. They just love you. I think that’s what an organization is supposed to do.”</p><p>Reese is scoring a career-high 15.4 points per game and, she believes — and her All-Star teammates back this up — elevating those around her in newfound fashion. She describes herself as being more confident and patient. Of course, the rebounding is still there, as ever. But about that? For a player whose reputation with the Sky was built on piling up double-doubles — for which both the team and Reese’s fans touted her a bit too much — the thinking has evolved.</p><p>“The double-doubles, they don’t matter unless we’re winning,” Reese said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-680000" name="image-680000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c8cb38c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/654c528/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5213892/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Former President Barack Obama poses for a selfie with WNBA All-Star Angel Reese during a practice at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago on Friday, July 24, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5213892/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/56808a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5213892/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3429x1924+0+181/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc2%2Fb2%2Ffc16698344738d1ce3c5f65fe83d%2Fwnba-all-star-basketball.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former President Barack Obama poses for a selfie with WNBA All-Star Angel Reese during a practice at the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago on Friday, July 24, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Paul Beaty/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>All-Stars Allisha Gray and Rhyne Howard score more than Reese, average more minutes and have put in more years getting the Dream pointed in the right direction. There are no signs Reese is under the impression she’s the main force driving the bus on this team, and that’s significant. So is her teammates’ full-on support of a newcomer who’s always had a strong taste for fame in addition to her on-court skills.</p><p>“She’s an amazing teammate, an amazing person, and one of the nicest people you could meet,” Gray said. “She’s a joy to be around, has so much positive energy, and you know what you’re going to get from her every day. I’ve had so much fun playing with her. Any time I have an interaction with Angel, it’s good.”</p><p>Howard called Reese “the piece we were missing.”</p><p>“Man, I love Angel,” Howard said. “I hope she’s a Dream for a long, long time. She’s super sweet, she’s super kind-hearted and she really knows how to keep basketball separate, and that’s a virtue that not everybody has, especially with teammates of her caliber. …</p><p>“She brings a lot of tenacity to our team, a virtue of ‘dog’ that we have to keep up with because she’s relentless. And she’s the best teammate. Even on her worst day, she makes sure somebody else is having their best.”</p><p>In her introductory press conference as a rookie at the Sky’s amateur-hour practice facility in Deerfield, Reese said she’d have to work her tail off just to make the team. In the end, even though things didn’t work out long-term, she did a whole lot better than that.</p><p>She felt “pretty good” being back in Chicago, but Atlanta has been a “dream come true, literally.”</p><p>Where does she hope to go from here?</p><p>“I mean, I think everybody always remembers the winner,” Reese said. “I want to be a winner, I want to be win that WNBA championship, I want to be an Olympian, and all the personal goals that come with [those things].</p><p>“But when I came to Atlanta, I just wanted to do whatever it takes to win. I didn’t know what my role was going to be or what it was going to look like. To be able to have my best year yet, to come and be so successful with this team, it just feels really, really good. I’m really, really happy.”</p><p>In other words, no drama.</p><p>An Obama could appreciate that.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/22/wnba-all-star-game-chicago-sky-united-center-caitlin-clark-paide-bueckers-angel-reese-breanna-stewart" >WNBA All-Star Game puts Sky’s fall from the top on all-too-vivid display</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/23/how-jerry-seinfeld-would-diagnose-the-skys-all-star-problem" >How Jerry Seinfeld would diagnose the Sky’s All-Star problem</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/24/obama-wnba-all-star-game-changemaker" target="_blank" >Obama drops in at WNBA event inspiring ninth-grade girls at presidential center</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: CBS NFL analyst Tony Romo arrested on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — CBS NFL analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has been arrested on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence.</p><p>According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office's arrest report, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests after getting stopped while driving south on Interstate 43 on Thursday. Sheriff's officials said Romo was taken into custody, booked and released.</p><p>He has a court appearance set for Sept. 21.</p><p>Romo went to high school about 35 miles from Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.</p><p>The 46-year-old Romo has been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during an NFL career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.</p><p>CBS had no comment regarding the arrest.</p><p>Romo remains the Cowboys' franchise leader in career touchdown passes with 248. He held the franchise record for career passing yards (34,183) until Dak Prescott overtook him last season.<br></p>

entries.title: Patrick Kane determined to help Blackhawks' new generation make the playoffs
entries.summary: <p>Patrick Kane understands the nostalgia angle of his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*xmr940*_up*MQ..*_ga*MzIyNTExODc3LjE3ODQ5MTcyMDI.*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODQ5MTcyMDIkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODQ5MTcyMDQkajU4JGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> return runs deep. It means a lot to him, too, to likely finish his career in the city where he carved his reputation as arguably the greatest American player in NHL history.</p><p>But he repeatedly emphasized Friday that nostalgia was not the sole factor behind his decision to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/23/blackhawks-patrick-kane-returns-nhl-free-agency?_gl=1*1m9ksfq*_up*MQ..*_ga*MzIyNTExODc3LjE3ODQ5MTcyMDI.*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODQ5MTcyMDIkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODQ5MTcyMDIkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >sign with the Hawks</a>. He's not returning to Chicago simply to "ride off into the sunset" down Madison Street.</p><p>"All [of] that is great, but that’s not why I’m here," Kane said. "That’s not the story. It's to come back, help this team win, help this team get in the playoffs."</p><p>Even with three Stanley Cup rings and 143 games of playoff experience, Kane hasn't gotten to enjoy postseason electricity much lately. Aside from the 2020 bubble, his only playoff appearance since 2017 came in the Rangers' disappointing first-round loss in 2023.</p><p>So choosing the Hawks over the Sabres — the Atlantic Division's top seed last season — represented a vote of confidence in the ultra-young Hawks as a "team on the rise," as well.</p><p>Kane and Connor Bedard forming a deadly offensive connection would certainly help the Hawks achieve their potential sooner. Kane said he texted Bedard some Thursday; they'll catch up more in the coming days.</p><p>"This will be my 20th year in the league, and I’ll probably see passes I’ve never seen before [by] playing with him," Kane said.</p><p>Kane has also been skating with Frank Nazar this summer and has been impressed by his work ethic and speed.</p><p>"I saw something where [Anton] Frondell is closer to my son in age than he is to me," he added. "That’s going to be a little bit different, but ... I love playing with young guys. It helps keep me fresh.</p><p>"I hope it's not the case where I’m coming in and they’re looking at me differently than they would any of their other teammates. I know there’s probably going to be certain circumstances where that happens. … I’m not saying I want to be just another guy on the team — I want to be a big leader and help the team take the next steps — but I want them to view me as their teammate."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" his explanation for not bringing back Kane or Jonathan Toews the past few years was that wanted the Hawks' young generation to develop their own leadership structure without instinctively deferring to legendary veterans.</p><p>He believes enough of that growth has now occurred — Bedard, for one, has taken full ownership of the team — that Kane's return won't disrupt any chemistry.</p><p>"These young players have established themselves," Davidson said. "They know what the NHL is like. They know their way around the league a little bit. So ... it’s the right time for [Kane] to come step in.</p><p>"There’s a lot of different things he can impart on our young players, not only how to become better players but even the unique experience of what it means ... to win as a Blackhawk. He’s one of the very select few that possesses that understanding."</p><p>So yes, nostalgia might not have been the sole factor, but it did hold some sway. </p><p>"[Returning to Chicago had] always been in the back of my mind," Kane said. "I don’t know if I ever thought it was possible, to be honest with you.</p><p>"Obviously, when Chicago showed their interest, it really got me interested, as well. You start looking at the team, the potential and where they’re at as a group. It really makes sense and seems like the perfect fit for me."</p><h3><b>Notes</b></h3><p>As for Toews, Davidson said he would love to "bring him back" too, presumably on a one-day contract to ceremoniously retire as a Hawk. A team spokesperson clarified that hasn't been discussed with Toews yet, so there aren't set plans. But it is a possibility.</p><p>Kane admitted he enjoyed reading Bedard's comments about "the excitement that he would have with me coming back," but he also felt bad that speculation about his future hung over Bedard's contract signing in any way.</p><p>Kane's return has unsurprisingly been a big marketing win for the Hawks. Thursday marked the biggest jersey sales day for their team store since the launch of the black jerseys last fall.</p><p>Demand for season-ticket memberships has also surged. Renewals had already exceeded 90% entering the offseason, per a team spokesperson, and new membership sales have doubled compared to this time last year, experiencing another 15% increase this week entries.title: LeBron James will close out his career with the Philadelphia 76ers
entries.summary: <p>PHILADELPHIA — LeBron James is heading to the Philadelphia 76ers.</p><p>The NBA's all-time leading scorer made the announcement on social media Friday, saying it will be his "last decision" and that it comes after he strongly considered retirement.</p><p>"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time," James said.</p><p>A four-time NBA champion, James wrote he was "done" when his 23rd NBA season ended and that it was his last with the Los Angeles Lakers.</p><p>"I was pretty sure I played my last game. I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game," James wrote. "I still truly love this game, and I have more to give."</p><p>The 41-year-old James is set to sign a modest $8 million, two-year contract with the Sixers, according to ESPN. He made nearly $53 million last season.</p><p>"I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family," James wrote. "What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning."</p><p>James celebrated his decision on Instagram with a career highlight reel set to Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill's "Dreams and Nightmares," the adopted sports anthem of city sports teams.</p><p>The video ends with the lyric, "hold up, wait a minute. Y'all thought I was finished?" and cuts to a 76ers' logo.</p><p>Fanatics already had his No. 23 jersey on sale for $125 with delivery not expected until the end of August.</p><p>Much as James did for Cleveland when he ended a 56-year championship drought for the city by leading the Cavaliers to the title in 2016, he can snap a lengthy title drought for the Sixers.</p><p>The Sixers went 45-37 last season and were swept in the second round by the NBA champion New York Knicks.</p><p>Most betting sites had the Sixers as 9-1 favorites to win the championship behind the Oklahoma City Thunder, the San Antonio Spurs and the New York Knicks, as of Friday afternoon.</p><p>James joins a 76ers team that has not won an NBA championship since 1983 and has not advanced out of the second round of the Eastern Conference playoffs since 2001.</p><p>The 76ers should boast one of the top starting fives in the NBA with fellow All-Stars Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, the 2024 NBA Finals MVP, a five-time All-Star and the league's fourth-leading scorer this past season acquired in a stunning offseason deal with the Celtics.</p><p>Maxey posted an Instagram story of him celebrating in a gym and yelling "what!? what?!" over the news while Brown wrote on X "#throwtheballup." Brown wrote that in his introductory note to Philadelphia, and it has already been branded on billboards throughout the city.</p><p>Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro even proclaimed Friday as LeBron James Day in the state.</p><p>Turned out with the Brown deal, new 76ers team president Mike Gansey — an Ohio prep basketball star with James — was just getting started with his summer of surprises.</p><p>No move, of course, hits like James' arrival.</p><p>He won his four NBA championships in stops with Cleveland, Miami and the Los Angeles Lakers. James left the Lakers after an eight-season run highlighted by the 2020 NBA title.</p><p>James is the NBA's oldest active player at 41 and the only player in league history to have a career spanning 23 seasons; this coming season will be his 24th. Speculation has been rampant for more than two months about his future, officially starting in May when the Lakers were eliminated from the NBA playoffs.</p><p>James' resume is beyond compare in NBA history. He's a 22-time All-Star, a 21-time All-NBA selection, a four-time Most Valuable Player, a four-time NBA Finals MVP, a three-time All-Star Game MVP, and was a member of the NBA's 75th anniversary team.</p><p>He's also coming off a season where he averaged 20.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 7.2 assists per game. For his career, he's averaged 26.8 points, 7.5 rebounds and 7.4 assists in more than 1,600 games.</p><p>James started his career in Cleveland in 2003 and spent seven seasons with the Cavaliers before heading to Miami for four seasons — where he won his first two NBA titles. He then returned to Cleveland for four more seasons, including that title run in 2016, and left in 2018 for the Lakers.</p><p>Cleveland and Miami were believed to be on James' radar again as he weighed this decision.</p><p>"Thank you LA. Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always home!" James wrote.</p><p>For the next two seasons, James' professional home is in Philadelphia.<br></p>

entries.title: Illinois added to CDC's investigation into diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak
entries.summary: <p>Illinois and three other states were added Friday to federal health officials’ investigation into a diarrhea-causing parasite that was first tied to shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants.</p><p>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention added Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania to the list of states with confirmed outbreaks of the disease cyclosporiasis. The other states that are part of the agency’s investigation are Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.</p><p>State and local public health officials have been interviewing people about the foods they ate within the two weeks of them becoming sick, the CDC said.</p><p>Across the nine states, at least 1,947 people have been infected with cyclospora and have reported eating at Taco Bell, according to the CDC.</p><p>No deaths have been reported in connection to the disease, and 98 people have been hospitalized, the CDC said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/14/illinois-reports-216-cases-of-diarrhea-inducing-cyclosporiasis" >What to know about diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“The true number of sick people in this multistate outbreak is likely higher than the number reported, and the outbreak may not be limited to the states with known illnesses,” CDC officials noted in a Friday update about the outbreak, which began June 22.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health reported as of Thursday that there have been 513 confirmed and probable cases of cyclosporiasis in the state. Of those, 39 people were hospitalized, 156 had recently traveled out of the country and 291 had recently traveled domestically.</p><p>More than 90 cases of the disease have been confirmed in Chicago as of Thursday, according to the city’s department of public health.</p><p>Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora. Infection often comes after eating fresh fruits and vegetables and can lead to watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, gas and nausea.</p><p>The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water.</p><p>Health officials urge people to follow typical food safety guidelines like washing hands and thoroughly washing and scrubbing fresh produce.</p>

entries.title: Michael Conforto thriving as Cubs’ pinch-hitter extraordinaire: ‘I don’t really know how he does that’
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — Pinch-hitting is hard. <b>Michael Conforto</b> is making it look easy.</p><p>“I don’t really know how he does that, to be totally honest,” second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said Wednesday. “It feels like he’s either homering or on the verge of it and [has] done it in really big moments for us, too.”</p><p>Conforto’s latest trick was his fourth pinch-hit homer of the year, coming in Tuesday’s win and tying <b>Glenallen Hill</b>’s franchise mark for the most in a single season.</p><p>All in a day’s — or, to be more precise — a moment’s work for Conforto, the veteran of 11 big league seasons who’s thriving in a limited role, bringing a do-anything attitude to a team with championship aspirations.</p><p>“This is a player who’s accomplished a lot in his career,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “He’s been a starter, he’s signed big contracts, he’s a first-round pick, he was a big prospect.</p><p>“He’s confident yet very humble. That allows him to be good at the job that he’s currently in. He’s not wondering why he’s not playing, he’s just getting ready for the next time he’s going to play or going to contribute.”</p><p>Added during spring training, Conforto has bounced back from a rough season with the Dodgers — he hit .199 last year for the eventual champs — bringing an .809 OPS into Friday that stood as his best in half a decade.</p><p>His numbers as a pinch-hitter? He’s batting .333 with a 1.268 OPS.</p><p>“It’s always, ‘Can you find a player that can do this job and be successful at it?’” Counsell said Tuesday. “Michael has done a fabulous job at it, and you feel like it’s a real weapon to have somebody like that.</p><p>“All year, it feels like his biggest hits have been pinch hits. He’s got four homers, so they probably have. It’s a really nice weapon, and it’ll be really useful, hopefully, the rest of the season.”</p><p>Those results go hand in hand with the positive contributions he’s made off the field, making it perhaps not so surprising that the Dodgers, apparently, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/11/cubs-michael-conforto-stats-lineup-dansby-swanson-craig-counsell-moises-ballesteros" >wish he never left</a>.</p><p>“Behind the scenes, what people don’t get to see, he’s so much at the heart of the fun that this team is having,” Hoerner said. “He’s been everything we could have hoped for and more.”</p><h3><b>Hollowell’s hurling</b></h3><p>Right-hander <b>Gavin Hollowell</b> has found himself among the contingent of Cubs relievers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/08/cubs-bullpen-ninth-inning-stats-jacob-webb-ryan-rolison-daniel-palencia-trent-thornton-tyler-ferguson" >thriving in unexpected roles</a> amid the team’s pitching injuries.</p><p>Hollowell came into Friday with seven straight scoreless appearances, and his 0.87 ERA since June 16 is one of the 30 lowest in baseball during that span among pitchers who have thrown at least 10 innings.</p><p>“Gavin’s somebody that’s really benefitted from the opportunity,” Counsell said Friday. “Basically all of last year, the first two months [of this season], he just wasn’t getting big-moment opportunities because of who else was on the team.</p><p>“[June 24 against the Mets], that was the first significant situation that he had pitched in, just because of where we had gotten to in terms of available pitchers. And he’s really taken that and run with it.”</p><h3><b>Pitchers on the mend</b></h3><p>Lefty reliever <b>Hoby Milner</b> and righty starter <b>Edward Cabrera</b> will throw live batting-practice sessions with Class A South Bend this weekend as they work back from injury.</p><p>Milner, out since an appendectomy last month, is slated to head to Triple-A Iowa after for a minor league rehab assignment.</p><p>Cabrera, coming back from a strained hamstring, is also due for minor league rehab work with the I-Cubs, which will come after rejoining the big league team in St. Louis.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: House Democrats may need policy change to properly handle complaints
entries.summary: <p>By now you’ve probably read at least something about the scandals surrounding former state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield.</p><p>In a nutshell, a young female district office staffer alleged Benton sexually harassed her in 2023. Two of House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch top staffers asked her to file a complaint with the legislative inspector general, but she refused. Welch’s caucus committee, Democrats for the Illinois House, then contributed $1.4 million to Benton’s reelection campaign.</p><p>Earlier this year, Welch quietly kicked Benton out of the House Democratic caucus, and stripped Benton of all his committee assignments and staff access. Then, in early July, Welch announced that he had received the legislative inspector general’s report and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/02/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-harry-benton-resign-misconduct-report" >called on Benton to resign</a> or be expelled from the House. Benton <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/03/plainfield-state-rep-harry-benton-resigns-amid-allegations-of-misconduct" >stepped down</a>.</p><p>Subsequent reporting by the Chicago Tribune found that Benton had made some highly inappropriate comments to a female lobbyist, which was also reported to the legislative inspector general. The Tribune also tracked down the former female staffer, who detailed Benton’s behavior but also said that when she’d subsequently asked Welch for career advice, he suggested they meet at a local restaurant’s bar.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Welch went into damage control and met privately with most of his members in groups. Some of his members were skeptical of his answers, and his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/23/benton-report-sexual-harassment-chris-welch-springfield" >future is at least somewhat uncertain</a>.</p><p>One member asked, for example, if any other stories would come out about him. He said that since he didn’t realize he had made the young woman uncomfortable by posting “heart eyes” emojis on her online photos and suggesting a meeting in a swanky bar, he had no idea if more might come out.</p><p>Another member pointed out that Welch was willing to meet with the young woman, but House Democrats are regularly told to meet with staff if they have an issue.</p><p>If House Democrats are looking for ways to prevent another fiasco, they could make a policy change that might help.</p><p>One structural problem is that House district office employees, like that young woman, do not have the right to expect the chamber’s Human Resource Office will do anything for them.</p><p>For the last several years, individual House members have been directly in charge of their district office operations. Their district staff, unlike legislative policy or clerk staff, do not work for and are not controlled by the House Speaker’s office.</p><p>And that means if a problem arises at the district level, the person responsible for resolving the issue is the House member. Complaints are supposed to go to the member, who is in charge of resolving them.</p><p>But if you’re a district staffer being sexually harassed by your employer, that is not an ideal system, to say the least.</p><p>According to the House clerk’s office, district office employees are given the option of talking to the chief of staff, the chief legal counsel, the legislative inspector eneral, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Illinois Department of Human Rights.</p><p>They can also go to the Human Resource office. But that office is designed to only cover employees of the House Speaker. They can offer advice, but they have no real authority over district-level employees.</p><p>It just makes no sense that legislators act as their own HR officers. And it also doesn’t seem fair to subject these district staffers to intimidating and even expensive legal processes when they have a complaint.</p><p>I get that members want autonomy over their staffs without direct interference from the speaker’s office, but that’s exactly what happened with Benton when Welch’s chief of staff and chief counsel swooped in to meet with the young woman who accused Benton of going way over the line.</p><p>And while I don’t believe the evidence in this case shows that Welch’s former chief of staff and chief legal counsel did anything wrong, those officers have a built-in conflict of interest.</p><p>It seems like common sense to send district staffers to an office which has experience working with these sorts of issues, instead of directing them to a quasi-judicial process that will essentially involve interrogation. The state Senate, by the way, allows district office staff full access to its Human Relations office.</p><p>Other ideas have also surfaced, including extending the one-year statute of limitations on reporting sexual harassment. Rep. Stephanie Kifowit, D-Oswego, suggested that all staff should be allowed to join a union.</p><p>This has to stop.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3f0000" name="module-3f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Cubs’ trade-deadline shopping list obvious, but do they have prospects necessary to win over sellers?
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — It’s no secret what the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>, clear buyers at the trade deadline, are shopping for this summer.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/21/cubs-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-tarik-skubal-rumors-pitching-injuries-bullpen-trent-thornton-phil-maton" target="_blank" >They need pitching</a>.</p><p>But they won’t be the only team seeking an upgrade. Do they have what it takes to persuade sellers to part with their pitchers?</p><p>‘‘It’s been a really good season so far for our system, position players in particular,’’ team president Jed Hoyer said a week ago. ‘‘We’ve had a lot of real breakouts, which has been good.</p><p>‘‘That isn’t talking about a desire to trade [away from that group], but it’s been really positive from a breakout standpoint, from a position-player performance standpoint. That’s super-important. That’s the future.’’</p><p>The Cubs called up one of those notable performers Friday, bringing their No. 11 prospect, utility player James Triantos, to the majors.</p><p>It was a nice reward for Triantos, the Cubs’ second-round draft choice five years ago, who has bounced back from a .684 OPS in 102 games last season at Triple-A Iowa to a .784 number in 88 games this season.</p><p>‘‘I learned a lot about myself last year,’’ Triantos said Friday. ‘‘You learn more about yourself when you fail than when you do well.</p><p>‘‘It could be a blessing in disguise. It isn’t how I wanted it to go last year. But I learned a lot, and now I’m a better player because of it.’’</p><p>If the idea is for Triantos — whom the Cubs are confident deploying as a second baseman, third baseman and left fielder — to impress any interested parties before the deadline Aug. 3, the opportunities will be minimal. That’s no surprise, given this is an entrenched position-player group chasing a place in the postseason.</p><p>‘‘There’s not a lot of playing time for this [roster] spot,’’ manager Craig Counsell said, ‘‘and that’s going to be the same situation for James. We’ll see what happens in this stretch of no days off, but [there’s] likely not going to be a lot of playing time.’’</p><p>Might we count Triantos among the candidates to head the other way in a potential deadline deal?</p><p>There has been speculation about another utility player, one with much more big-league experience, but Matt Shaw won’t have a chance to impress before the deadline. He still is working to get over the hump in his recovery from a sprained hand that has sidelined him since late last month.</p><p>Shaw’s roster spot has become a revolving door of young players. Outfielder Kevin Alcantara was sent down as Triantos came up, and that rotation will continue, Counsell said.</p><p>It was a strategy the Cubs used a year ago with Alcantara, catcher/designated hitter Moises Ballesteros and outfielder Owen Caissie, hoping to keep them from rusting on the big-league bench. But no trade involving any of those prospects materialized at the deadline last year, with Hoyer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/31/2025-trade-deadline-cubs-prez-jed-hoyer-balks-at-asking-price-for-frontline-starter-adds-four-players" target="_blank" >balking at the high price of pitching</a>.</p><p>After a brief playoff run, Hoyer made that move in the winter, dealing Caissie for right-hander Edward Cabrera, whose extended absence with a hamstring injury has helped intensify the Cubs’ current pitching need.</p><p>Infielder Pedro Ramirez, who started the season among the Cubs’ top-rated prospects, has assumed a more permanent reserve role than might have been initially expected and has impressed in limited action.</p><p>‘‘There’s a lot to like,’’ Counsell said of Ramirez. ‘‘For a 22-year-old to come up and play sporadically and be on the bench and still be a contributor, it’s been fun to watch.’’</p><p>No farmhand has opened more eyes than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/23/cubs-prospect-josiah-hartshorn-mlb-top-100-prospects-home-runs-stats-draft-signing-bonus-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-jayden-murray-trade-astros" target="_blank" >outfielder Josiah Hartshorn</a>, whose big season at Class A has him as the Cubs’ highest-rated prospect, just ahead of Double-A infielder Jefferson Rojas.</p><p>Might there be a greater urgency for Hoyer and the front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" target="_blank" >to be aggressive this summer</a>? Or will the high price of pitching once more deter the Cubs from dealing away part of their future?</p><p>Most important: Do the Cubs even have the kinds of pieces it would take to swim in those waters?</p><p>‘‘The players that people were talking about as trade chips at this point, those are the players that next year may be impacting us,’’ Hoyer said. ‘‘You always have to keep that in mind. I think we have a lot of guys that can help us here pretty quickly.’’</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true"
