entries.title: Is Caitlin Clark the best point guard at All-Star weekend? Relax — she's definitely one of them
entries.summary: <p>Caitlin Clark flops too much. She talks too <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/06/11/caitlin-clark-holds-two-truths-about-her-competitive-fire-can-we" >much trash</a>. She's overly dramatic in campaigning for calls.</p><p>Those are the casual reasons to root against her. Then there are the heavier ones. Clark's stardom has become a mirror for larger societal arguments. Is the spotlight on her fair? Does she take responsibility for her platform? Is the league grateful enough for her popularity?</p><p>"I would be lying to you if I didn't say it's a little bit exhausting to constantly have to deal with things," Clark said. "A lot of the time it's very distracting from the product and the game."</p><p>Clark is right. With all the surrounding noise, it’s easy to forget there's an exciting basketball debate to be had: Who's the best point guard in town for the All-Star Game this weekend?</p><p>Clark entered the league as perhaps the most-hyped prospect in league history when the Fever chose her No. 1 in the 2024 draft. Three seasons in, she has mostly delivered — an All-Star every year, electric in transition and lethal in the two-man game with Aliyah Boston.</p><p>But her rise has been choppy, slowed by injuries that kept her out of most of her sophomore season and have limited her minutes this season. Meanwhile Paige Bueckers, the top pick in the 2025 draft, keeps getting better.</p><p>Voted by general managers as the player most would want to build a franchise around, Bueckers has backed that up by pulling the Wings from last place straight into title contention.</p><p>And now there's a newer challenger: Lynx rookie Olivia Miles. The player who likely should have been the No. 1 pick in the 2026 draft has her own swagger, too.</p><p>Miles called Clark an "incredible player" and said she's excited to team up for the weekend. But she isn't conceding anything.</p><p>Asked about her mindset every time she steps on the court, Miles sat up a little taller.</p><p>"No one can touch me," Miles said. "It's not cocky at all. It's just the thought you have to have to be a killer. If you step on the floor and you doubt yourself, you already lost."</p><p>Like everyone else around the league, Clark has taken notice of Miles. She's been a fan of her game since her college days. Clark's word for Miles' style: flawless.</p><p>"It's fast in the right moments, it's slow in the right moments," Clark said. "You can see her creative juices flowing on the floor. I think that's the thing about being a point guard. I always tell people I'm really not a creative person, but my creativity just comes out on the court."</p><p>It might just be the golden age for the creative point guard after a lull that followed the primes of legends like Lindsay Whalen, Sue Bird and Courtney Vandersloot.</p><p>Asked to compare her game to Clark's and Miles', Bueckers pointed to differences in what makes them most dangerous: Clark's deep range and Miles' ability to pressure the rim.</p><p>"I'm kind of in the middle," Bueckers said with a smile.</p><p>In the middle, but far from average. Heading into the break, the mid-range master trails only four-time MVP A'ja Wilson in the betting odds for the MVP race.</p><p>Both Bueckers and Clark helped draw out what really separates the trio: Clark's audacity, Miles' paces, and Bueckers' control of the game.</p><p>The common thread, Bueckers said, is confidence. Each stepped onto a WNBA floor and took ownership of her franchise from Day 1.</p><p>All three have drawn massive attention, though no player deals with the spotlight quite like Clark.</p><p>"There's going to be some people that love you and some people that hate you, and that's just the reality of the world when you get into a position like this," Clark said. "That's also a good thing for the game. Not everyone's going to be your biggest fan. They can love different players. They can support different players."</p><p>So take your pick — Clark, Bueckers or Miles. Argue about it all you want. Just try to remember to have fun with it.</p><p>And if you need a refresher on how, listen to Courtney Williams — who happily gave up point guard duties when the Lynx drafted Miles — talk about the new generation.</p><p>"They so raw," Williams said. "They overly raw. I tell Liv all the time like, 'Yo, you make me feel like, yo, could I go do that? Why don't I be doing that?' They just make the game look so easy. The league is definitely in great hands."</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: 111 years later, S.S. Eastland disaster victims remembered
entries.summary: <p>Holding a black-and-white photo of his great aunt, Scott Long leaned over the Chicago Riverwalk railing Friday and scattered a handful of flowers into the river, honoring a life the S.S. Eastland disaster claimed 111 years ago.</p><p>Long, 62, took a photograph of the portrait of his great aunt, Mabel Deichmann, held against the backdrop of the river where she died on July 24, 1915.</p><p>Deichmann was 21 when the Eastland, a passenger steamship, rolled onto its side while docked along the Chicago River, killing 844 people. It remains Chicago’s deadliest single-day disaster.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://eastlanddisaster.org/" target="_blank" >Eastland Disaster Historical Society</a> marked the 111th anniversary with a ceremony along the Riverwalk between La Salle and Clark.</p><p>Long’s family has carried the story through generations.</p><p>“My grandfather, my grandmother, her sister and my uncle were on the Eastland,” Long said.</p><p>More than 2,500 passengers, most of them Western Electric factory workers and their families, boarded the Eastland on an overcast Saturday morning for the company’s annual picnic.</p><p>Minutes after boarding, before the ship ever left the dock, the overloaded, top-heavy Eastland tipped over. Many passengers were trapped below the deck as the water flowed in, prompting a frantic rescue by first responders and bystanders.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div The excursion steamer rolled over while partially tied to the dock. More than 800 people were killed, most within a few feet of shore. It was one of the worst maritime disasters in U.S. history. The Eastland was filled with picnic-bound employees of the Western Electric Company and their families. Investigators determined the top-heavy ship’s lack of seaworthiness was a primary cause.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jun Fujita/Chicago Daily News</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Long’s grandfather helped his wife and young son off the ship then climbed back aboard, again and again, in search of Deichmann, who had boarded with a different group of Western Electric employees.</p><p>“Each time he went to look for her, he rescued someone,” Long said. “He rescued three or four women.”</p><p>Later that day, Deichmann’s body was identified at the Second Regiment Armory, on the Washington Boulevard on the Near West Side, which was used as a temporary morgue.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div> </div><p>Their grandmother had eagerly boarded what seemed like an enormous ship, but because the upper deck was crowded, the family found seats on the middle deck. When the Eastland rolled over, they were trapped for hours inside the vessel before rescuers pulled them through a porthole.</p><p>Wachholz’s grandmother treaded water for “many hours” and held onto “whatever debris” floated by.</p><p>“She saw things that were not pleasant at all for a young girl,” Barbara Wachholz said.</p><p>“But what she said gave her inspiration was the fact that when the ship rolled over, they, fortunately, were on the side that was facing up,” Wachholz said. “And she could look through the porthole and see the sky. And she just had such hope that she would be able to pull through.”</p><p>“If our 14-year-old grandmother had not survived, my sister, Susan, and I would not be here today. And that goes for so many other families,” Wachholz said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-750000" name="image-750000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/828fb12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2F19%2Feeaf87314c2a9c8d0398ad796999%2Feastland-260725-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4d40cc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2F19%2Feeaf87314c2a9c8d0398ad796999%2Feastland-260725-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccc6dbc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2e%2F19%2Feeaf87314c2a9c8d0398ad796999%2Feastland-260725-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Barbara Decker Wachholz, a co-founder of the Eastland Disaster Historical Society, speaks during a ceremony commemorating those who perished in the S.S. all boarded.</p><p>“The ship beneath their feet was a fragile illusion,” Conlon said, describing a “top heavy” vessel “plagued by stability issues” that were ignored by the ship company, crew members
